News.title: Teacher who sexually assaulted pupil wants sentence cut over PTSD – but fails
News.content:
Teacher who sexually assaulted pupil wants sentence cut over PTSD – but fails

Teacher and Army veteran Simon Taylor - who was jailed in January for sexually assaulting a pupil - has lost his bid to shorten his sentence after claiming his PTSD was not taken into sufficient account

View 2 Images Simon Taylor was jailed for four years and six months for sexually assaulting a 'vulnerable' pupil (Image: PA)

A former teacher has failed in his bid to shorten his prison term for sexually assaulting a "vulnerable" pupil - after the Court of Appeal rejected his claim that his PTSD should have been given greater weight during his sentencing.

Army veteran Simon Taylor was jailed for four years and six months at Norwich Crown Court in January for multiple offences against the teenage girl. Today, Taylor lost his bid to challenge the length of his sentence at the Court of Appeal in London.

The offending took place over more than two years, beginning while the victim was a pupil at Hethersett Academy in Norfolk, where Taylor worked as a teacher, and continuing after she had left the school.

After the victim reported the offending, Taylor later admitted two counts of sexual assault, including one incident that took place in his car, as well as an offence of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust and two counts of sexual communication with a child.

View 2 Images The Court of Appeal dismissed Taylor's appeal bid (Image: Xinhua/REX/Shutterstock)

During the appeal hearing, Taylor’s lawyers argued that the sentence was too high and that sentencing judge Andrew Shaw had failed to give sufficient weight to mitigating factors, including Taylor's post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

His lawyers said his PTSD stemmed from having part of his right leg amputated after his vehicle was hit by a roadside bomb in 2009 while he was serving in Afghanistan.

But three senior judges dismissed the appeal bid, stating that the victim was "particularly vulnerable" and that Taylor continued his offending despite being warned about his behaviour.

Mr Justice Goose, sitting with Lord Justice Foxton and Judge Sylvia De Bertodano, said: "The complainant was a vulnerable child and had been targeted, manipulated and groomed into believing that the applicant was the only adult who cared for her."

He continued: "The judge correctly increased the sentence to reflect the totality of the offending, which in our judgment required a significant uplift from its starting point."

He added: "We are not persuaded that such a sentence can be described as excessive or wrong in principle. The offences were committed against the background of the applicant’s position at a school, one of very high trust."

The judge also said that Taylor contacted the girl on the school’s messaging platform and deleted messages to "destroy" evidence.

Article continues below

Taylor, who watched proceedings from HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, made no reaction as his appeal bid was dismissed.

In January, alongside his prison sentence, Taylor was ordered to sign the sex offenders register, made subject to an indefinite sexual harm prevention order and a restraining order, and barred from working with children.

News.title: Anyone who cooks bacon or steak urged to avoid mistake that makes it 'chewy and tough'
News.content:
Anyone who cooks bacon or steak urged to avoid mistake that makes it 'chewy and tough'

An expert has shared the simple pan trick that changes everything about the way bacon and steak taste - and once you try it, you'll never go back.

View 3 Images There's nothing better than perfectly crispy bacon (Image: Brandon Polifrone via Getty Images)

It's the kind of cooking mistake that most of us have been making for years without even realising it. You fire up the hob, heat the pan until it's smoking hot, and throw in your bacon or steak, just like every recipe tells you to.

‌



But according to one professional, that single step could be the reason your meat never quite tastes as good as it should.

‌



Niall McCusker, an expert at specialist butcher Campbells Meat, says the temperature of your pan before the meat goes in makes all the difference - and for bacon and fatty cuts of steak, starting hot is the worst thing you can do.

‌



"The way you cook your meat will ultimately affect the taste and the texture," he said.

View 3 Images Certain higher-fat meats should always be cooked in a cold pan (Image: Getty)

Why a hot pan is bad for bacon and steak

It might seem odd, but the key to perfectly cooked bacon and steak lies in starting with a cold pan. While a red-hot pan works well for lean cuts like chicken breasts, pork chops or lean steaks, it's not great for high-fat cuts like bacon and marbled steak.

‌



The reason comes down to fat. When you drop fatty meat into a searingly hot pan, the outside of the meat seizes up almost instantly. The fat doesn't have time to render down properly, meaning you end up with chewy, tough meat and fat that's either burnt on the outside or still rubbery in the middle.

"These foods have a high fat content, so you need to know how to render the fat and get it nice and crispy without burning the meat," Niall explained.

"Starting off with a cold pan lets the fat slowly melt as it turns into a liquid. That cooks off the fat and gives you that flavour without burning the meat. It also results in a more tender texture, as it hasn't tightened up from cooking on a high heat."

‌



In other words, a cold pan gives the fat time to do its job - basting the meat in its own juices as the temperature gradually rises, producing a richer flavour and a far more satisfying texture.

How to cook bacon on the hob

For the best results with bacon, lay the rashers flat in a cold, dry frying pan - no oil needed, as the fat in the bacon will provide more than enough. Place the pan over a medium heat and let the bacon cook slowly, turning occasionally.

As the pan heats up, you'll hear the sizzle begin and the fat will start to render, turning golden and crisp. This gradual process is what gives you bacon that's properly caramelised and full of flavour, rather than singed on the outside with a chewy, undercooked fat strip running through the middle.

‌



Depending on the thickness of your rashers and how crispy you like them, the whole process should take around six to eight minutes. Thicker, smoked back bacon will take a little longer than thin streaky rashers, which crisp up quickly.

Once cooked, transfer to a plate lined with kitchen roll to absorb any excess grease before serving.

View 3 Images Bacon is a breakfast, lunch and dinner staple here in the UK (Image: Getty)

‌



How to cook steak properly on the hob

The same cold-pan principle applies to fatty cuts of steak. Cuts with visible fat running through or around them - such as ribeye, sirloin or T-bone - benefit from starting in a cold pan.

Before you begin, take the steak out of the fridge at least 20 to 30 minutes before cooking to allow it to come up to room temperature. This helps it cook more evenly throughout.

Pat the steak dry with kitchen paper - this is crucial, as any surface moisture will steam the meat rather than sear it, preventing that golden-brown crust from forming.

‌



Season generously with salt and freshly ground black pepper on both sides. Some chefs prefer to season just before cooking; others salt the steak up to an hour in advance to allow the seasoning to penetrate the meat more deeply.

Place the seasoned steak in a cold pan, then turn the heat to medium-high. As the pan heats up and the fat begins to render, the steak will start to sear. Leave it undisturbed so a proper crust can develop.

For a steak around 2.5cm thick, cook for roughly two to three minutes per side for medium rare, adding a minute or two per side for medium or well-done. If the steak has a thick fat cap around the edge, hold it upright using tongs for a minute or two to render and crisp that fat fully.

Article continues below

Don't skip the resting stage

One of the most overlooked steps in cooking steak - and one that makes a significant difference to the finished result - is resting the meat after cooking. Once the steak comes off the heat, place it on a warm plate and leave it to rest for at least five minutes before cutting into it.

During cooking, the juices in the meat are pushed towards the centre by the heat. Resting allows those juices to redistribute throughout the steak, so that when you do slice into it, they stay in the meat rather than running out onto the plate. Skip this step and even a perfectly cooked steak will be drier than it should be.

News.title: Crete wildfires live: Rethymno in flames amid mass evacuations on Greek islands
News.content:
Flames are tearing across Greek Islands, forcing the evacuation of entire villages on Crete, Paros and Andros as wildfires continue to sweep across Europe

Raging wildfires have taken hold across several Greek islands, forcing villages to be evacuated as firefighters struggle to contain the flames.

Wildfires in the Rethymno area of the south of Crete are burning "out of control on all fronts", with firefighting aircraft unable to be deployed due to strong winds and thousands of people evacuated, including tourists. Urgent evacuation orders have also been issued for parts of Paros and Andros.

Three firefighters have died in Greece, with two becoming trapped in a vehicle while tackling flames in Crete. Meanwhile, Europe's emergency response chief warned the entire continent could be engulfed as intense blazes rage in France, Spain and Portugal.

"Italy will face risk at the beginning of August, and we will need to see what will happen with the Iberian Peninsula, because if (it is) there as well, we will have all Europe on fire," she said yesterday.

News.title: Suffolk fire live: Nuclear plant monitoring ‘unprecedented’ wildfire destroying rare bird habitat
News.content:
A wildfire is raging in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk where evacuations have been ordered - the blaze is close to three nuclear plant sites, and has burned an area the size of 140 football pitches

Hundreds of people were evacuated overnight after a wildfire erupted in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, with firefighters still battling to bring it under control today.

Temperatures have soared into the 30s in southern England today, doing little to help the huge emegrency response. The fire has now burned an area the size of 140 football pitches, posing a risk to holiday parks and the UK's largest nuclear power plant. Some 200 caravans were evacuated, with holidaymakers woken up by banging on their doors.

EDF says it is "continuing to monitor the situation" at the Sizewell B power plant, while staff at Sizewell C - a planned nuclear power station located 10 miles from the fire - say there is a "low risk".

There is also concern for wildlife in the area, after nature reserve RSPB Minsmere announcing its closure this morning. RSPB Suffolk area manager Adam Rowlands said the land was home to rare wildlife including nightjars - and it could take "more than a decade" for the habitat to recover.

The fire spread across Dunwich Heath due to a change in wind conditions overnight, and there are fears more changes could worsen the situation. Chief Fire Officer Jon Lacey said it was a "very dynamic and fast-paced incident", adding: "I wouldn't say the fire is surrounded and we're on top of it because it moves faster than we're able to deal with it."

News.title: Lifelong poker player becomes world's oldest paid pro - aged 100
News.content:
Lifelong poker player becomes world's oldest paid pro - aged 100

Ivor Parker has spent his life playing the game after first picking up a deck of cards when he was just 14

View 4 Images Ivor Parker playing poker aged 100 (Image: Doug Peters/PinPep / SWNS)

A lifelong poker player has become the world’s oldest paid professional - at the age of 100.

‌



Ivor Parker has spent his life playing the game after first picking up a deck of cards when he was just 14. He played his first hand in a pub in Boston, Lincs in 1940, giving him 86 years’ worth of experience on the tables.

‌



Over the years, he has built his knowledge of the game - claiming every successful player needs patience, resilience, strategy and a love of competition. He said poker remains one of the few competitive pursuits where experience, composure and decision-making continue to matter regardless of age.

‌



View 4 Images Ivor started playing poker aged 14 (Image: Doug Peters/PinPep / SWNS)

Ivor, from Ab Kettleby, Leicestershire, has now been signed by GGPoker as a full-time ambassador He kicked off his tenure at a VIP event with Grosvenor Casinos on the eve of the Goliath 2026 poker tournament.

He said: “I’ve loved poker for as long as I can remember. I started playing when I was 14. I loved the game straight away and I’ve never really looked back. I've played poker all over the world, especially during the war. Every game is different, every table has its own stories and you’re always learning something new.”

‌



Alongside his love of poker, Ivor - who has been married twice and has five children - worked as a production operative for East Midlands Farmer until he was 98.

View 4 Images Ivor Parker taking part in poker tournament (Image: Doug Peters/PinPep / SWNS)

Ivor added: “Poker today is so different to when I started, it's so much more strategic now and there are so many brilliant players, especially here today. If I think about it, I’ve played poker with hundreds of people, some of them my really good friends, who sadly have all gone now. I think poker has kept me sharp and I'm thankful for that.”

‌



Leah Hauer, GGPoker brand ambassador, said: “Poker rewards patience, discipline and good decision-making, and those are qualities that anyone can develop. Sharing the table with Ivor has been incredibly inspiring, and it shows exactly why Poker is such a unique game, there's always something to learn from the people sitting around you.”

View 4 Images Ivor says poker keeps him sharp (Image: Doug Peters/PinPep / SWNS)

Angela Martin, head of marketing at GGPoker, said: “Poker has always been about much more than cards. It’s about bringing people together, continually learning and challenging yourself. Ivor perfectly embodies everything we love about the game, and we're incredibly proud to welcome him to Team GGPoker as we head into Goliath.”

Article continues below

The tournament will see more than 6,000 players at Grosvenor Casino Coventry, transforming the city into the home of live poker.

News.title: Amazon drone on delivery crashes into garden just months after local feared 'it could hit a baby'
News.content:
Amazon drone on delivery crashes into garden just months after local feared 'it could hit a baby'

Amazon Prime air teams and firefighters were called to Beaumont Hill in Darlington, County Durham, when a drone delivering a package collided into a residential garden

View 5 Images Drones have been deployed in Darlington for a few months (file image)

An investigation has been launched after an Amazon drone delivering a package crashed into a garden - just a couple of months after locals expressed fears about potential accidents.

‌



Amazon and the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) have said they are investigating after the drone, part of the delivery giant's automated fleet, crashed in Beaumont Hill in Darlingon, County Durham. No one was injured in the incident, with Amazon concluding early on that the crash likely took place after the drone hit "an object extending above the roof of a moving vehicle".

‌



But it has realised the fears of some Darlington residents, who spoke out following the launch of the firm's first-ever UK-based drone delivery service in May. One even told us she was worried a drone could hit a baby or young child.

‌



Amazon launches drone service in UK with parcels delivered within two hours READ MORE :

Amazon robots will replace some 'manual' warehouse roles READ MORE :

View 5 Images Prime Air technicians came to retrieve the drone following the incident (Image: ChronicleLive)

Darlington is the only place outside the US where the retail giant is providing the drone delivery service. The scheme received approval from the Civil Aviation Authority for a trial until the end of the year.

John Peacock, who lives in the neighbourhood in the north of the town, told Chronicle Live he heard a loud noise early in the morning on Wednesday, believing initially that his neighbours were having work done on their property. After looking outside, he said he spotted the drone lying on the ground, its motors and propellers still running and "destroying themselves".

‌



He told ChronicleLive: "It wasn't huge but it's a substantial-sized body with a lot of energy, when the thing landed, it was very, very powerful. I don't think they're designed for an urban or semi rural environment, I'm not in favour of them at all."

Reporters from the publication who arrived at the scene noted that, despite the noise and disruption, there was little damage, being primarily confined to a small provet hedge. A spokesperson for Amazon said, following the incident the initial probe discovered the drone had responded as designed when encountering an obstacle.

View 5 Images The drone crash landed at a Darlington property (Image: ChronicleLive)

‌



They said: “While our investigation is ongoing, our initial assessment is that an object extending above the roof of a moving vehicle inadvertently came into contact with a Prime Air drone during delivery. Following the contact, the drone responded as designed and came safely to the ground. We are continuing to investigate and are working closely with the relevant regulatory authorities."

A spokesperson for the AAIB, also confirming the incident, said an "accident" took place when the drone encountered difficulties. They said: "An accident involving a drone that was delivering a package in Darlington was reported to the AAIB. An investigation has been launched, and we have begun making inquiries."

Darlington was chosen as the site of Amazon's first UK drone delivery service, Amazon Prime Air, on May 7 this year and sees drones deliver small ites weighing less than 5lb (2.2kg).

‌



View 5 Images Damage from the drone appears to have been limited to a privet hedge (Image: ChronicleLive)

The packages are sped to customers in a small, 7.5-mile radius from a local fulfilment centre, and they arrive in just under two hours. Similar services are currently operative in the US, where deliveries can be carried out in just over half an hour - around 36 minutes. But the new service has encountered resistance both in the UK and stateside.

But Darlington residents speaking earlier this year had outlined their fears about the service to the Mirror, saying following its rollout that they worried the technology could malfunction.

‌



Among those worried about the drones was Mary Warner, 56, who said at the time that she hadn't used the service. She said: "I would be very unhappy to see an airborne drone. They could run out of battery power due to human error and land on someone’s head, the worst case scenario being a baby. The noise would be quite unnerving."

View 5 Images Amazon said the drone was operating as intended (Image: ChronicleLive)

Not all residents were opposed to the service, however, with Majorie Dunn raving about the experience after having twice ordered items using Amazon Air. She told the Mirror: "I’m fortunate to live off the beaten track so have no worries about parcels being stolen.

Article continues below

"We also have plenty of green round us for a soft landing. I missed the first delivery as I wasn’t at home so made sure I was at home for the second. There was a loud buzzing and the drone appeared over outlet rooftop and hovered over the lawn before releasing the parcel. It did drop it but both parcels were safe. Then the drone quickly gained height and flew off. I enjoyed the new experience."

Amazon has insisted that its drones have been able to carry out hundreds of thousands of deliveries globally with "very few mishaps", despite a handful of previous crash incidents - again involving no injuries - in the US.

A spokesperson told the Mirror: "We won't cut corners. Prime Air systems are built with multiple safety features. Our MK30 drone has received Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) approval to fly Beyond Visual Line of Sight. This enables drones to navigate safely to their destinations and return, ensuring the safety of people, pets, and property."

News.title: National Lottery draw hits £377 MILLION in Britain's biggest ever jackpot
News.content:
National Lottery draw hits £377 MILLION in Britain's biggest ever jackpot

A record £377 million jackpot will be up for grabs on this weekend's National Lottery Powerball draw after the UK became the first country outside the US to enter

View 3 Images A UK record £377 million is up for grabs on this weekend's Powerball (Image: Doug Peters/PA Media Assignments)

National Lottery players will be in line to scoop a £377 million prize this weekend in the largest jackpot ever offered in a UK draw.

‌



The gigantic sum will be up for grabs on the Powerball - but there's one catch. If you win it, the money will be paid over 30 years, rather than in one lump sum. Britain became the first country outside the US and its territories to enter the Powerball earlier this month.

‌



The £377 million draw will be held in Miami, Florida at 11pm Saturday local time (4am Sunday BST). Players pick five numbers from 1 to 69 and a Powerball number from 1 to 26, and tickets cost £4. You have to match them all to take the top prize.

‌



View 3 Images US winners have the option to claim the prize in full - while it will be paid annually for British players (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Powerball winner suffered unexpected dark side after 40p ticket landed him £23m READ MORE :

Tickets can be purchased in shops or online, the same as existing National Lottery games such as the EuroMillions and Lotto. And like the other draws, you can also opt for a lucky dip if you'd rather not choose the numbers yourself.

UK players must buy their tickets before 11.55pm on Saturday to enter this weekend's draw. While Powerball winners in the US have the option to take the money straight away and have 50% shaved off, you can only receive it in annuity in the UK.

‌



National Lottery Allwyn said this would ensure that winners get the biggest jackpot possible. The jackpot is divided equally if there are multiple people with the same winning numbers - raising the prospect of money being shared across the pond.

View 3 Images A UK winner on the Florida draw would dwarf Joe and Jess Thwaite's £184 million EuroMillions win (Image: Rowan Griffiths / Daily Mirror)

Andy Carter, Senior Winners’ Advisor at Allwyn, operator of The National Lottery, said: "The Powerball jackpot now stands at a staggering £377M, this is mind-blowing money.

‌



"When jackpots reach these heights, it's impossible not to imagine the possibilities. From unforgettable experiences to lasting legacies, a prize of this size has the power to transform lives in extraordinary ways. Players have until 11.55pm on Saturday night to get their tickets.

"Playing any National Lottery game is about so much more than just a big win. Every week, players help raise around £33M for Good Cause projects that make a real difference to communities across the UK."

Britain's biggest ever lottery win to date came in July 2022, when an anonymous ticketholder scooped £195 million on the EuroMillions. The second-highest winners are Joe and Jess Thwaite, from Gloucester, a couple in their 40s who scooped up a then-record £184.3 million in May the same year with a Lucky Dip ticket.

Article continues below

Joe, a communications sales engineer, and Jess, who ran a hairdressing salon, both went to work on the day they found out about the win. Mrs Thwaite said a few days later: "I didn’t think it was real to be honest. I still don’t think that it’s real."

EuroMillions jackpots are capped at €250 million (£215 million), but there are no upper limits on Powerball prizes. The largest US win ever was a $2.04 billion (£1.5 billion) jackpot scooped by Powerball player Edwin Castro in California in November 2022.

He was later taken to court by a man who alleged he stole his ticket one day before the draw, but the claim was thrown out by a Los Angeles judge. Mr Castro's $3.8 million ocean front Malibu home was destroyed in last year's California wildfires. He has since bought more land ravaged by the disaster, and has promised to develop the sites to build family homes.

News.title: Sugar warning as professors share myth many UK households believe
News.content:
Sugar warning as professors share myth many UK households believe

Two of the UK's most prominent nutrition experts have sought to clear up one of the biggest misconceptions when it comes to sugar

View 3 Images Professor Tim Spector (Image: Zoe - Youtube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yHv2NLaS7kw)

Two of Britain's best-known nutrition experts say millions have been left confused by treating all sugar as equally harmful. Professor Tim Spector and Professor Sarah Berry insist the sugar naturally found in fruit should not be lumped together with the refined sugar added to cakes, biscuits, sweets and fizzy drinks.

‌



The pair set out to bust some of the biggest myths surrounding sugar in the latest episode of the ZOE Science & Nutrition podcast. ZOE is a nutrition science company that combines cutting-edge nutrition research with personalised dietary advice through its app and home testing kits.

‌



Prof Spector is its scientific co-founder and one of the world's 100 most-cited scientists, while Professor Berry is ZOE's Chief Scientist and Professor of Nutrition at King's College London, where she led the world's largest study into how blood sugar responds to food.

‌



Prof Spector's words come as researchers today claimed cutting babies' sugar intake could slash their risk of dementia decades later. The new study found those exposed to wartime sugar rationing before birth and during their first two years of life were around 20% less likely to develop dementia than others.

View 3 Images People should focus on cutting back on added or "free" sugars (Image: by Chakarin Wattanamongkol via Getty Images)

Prof Berry said many people wrongly assume fruit is unhealthy simply because it contains sugar. "I absolutely disagree with the narrative that fruit, just because it's high in sugar, is bad for us," she said.

‌



“We cannot think of sugar and fruit in the same way.” She explained that the sugar in whole fruit is "intrinsic" – naturally enclosed within the fruit's structure alongside fibre, vitamins and hundreds of beneficial plant compounds. That means an orange is processed by the body very differently from a glass of orange juice.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Professor Berry pointed to randomised controlled trials comparing whole fruit, fruit puree, fruit juice and equivalent amounts of refined sugar. The evidence consistently shows whole fruit delivers the greatest health benefits.

‌



Fruit puree comes next because it still contains the fruit's nutrients. Fruit juice performs less well after much of the fibre has been removed. Refined sugar has the poorest health outcomes.

She also challenged the idea that smoothies are unhealthy, saying they remain a good source of fibre and beneficial plant compounds – provided the pulp is left in rather than strained out. Professor Spector admitted his own views had changed over the years.

View 3 Images Tim Spector is an expert in gut health (Image: Getty)

‌



"I was brought up on orange juice. I gave it to my kids. It was part of our family," he said.

"But orange juice is essentially full of sugar. It's got some vitamins, got potassium, but essentially a lot of it is this sugar that is going from the fruit. Not eating it as the whole orange, it's being released much quicker than you would get eating an orange, and you're not getting that fibre to also dampen down that absorption.

“So it's a really unnatural sugar rush you're getting from orange juice. Delicious though it might be, it should be a rare treat, not a daily option.”

Article continues below

The podcast also tackles several of the biggest questions surrounding sugar, including whether it really causes diabetes, whether athletes need sugar for energy, why some of the healthiest foods naturally contain sugar and whether cutting it out altogether is the right approach.

Instead, the experts argue people should focus on cutting back on added or "free" sugars while continuing to eat whole fruit, where the sugar is packaged together with fibre and nutrients that fundamentally change how the body processes it. Listen to the whole podcast here.

News.title: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures reveal
News.content:
There has been a large rise in the number of offenders being recalled to prisons in England and Wales having been released on licence, new government figures show.

There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.

The figures follow government schemes to release a number of offenders early in an effort to ease prison overcrowding.

The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said offenders released on licence face strict conditions "and can be hauled back to prison if they break these rules".

Cassia Rowland, from the Institute for Government think tank, said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.

"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.

News.title: Watch: Giant iceberg turns over near  Greenland's coast
News.content:
A massive iceberg was seen turning over off the coast of Greenland, near Ilulissat.

Video captured by an eyewitness showed the moment the iceberg turned over, creating waves close to the coastal city.

Ilulissat is home to the Unesco listed Ilulissat Icefjord and is located on the west coast of the island.

News.title: Four people die trying to cross Channel in small boats
News.content:
Four people died trying to cross the Channel in small boats overnight, French officials have said.

One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, with a one-year-old child among those injured.

Separately, three people were found dead aboard a small boat early on Thursday after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.

French officials confirmed their deaths after several hundred people crossed the Channel into the UK on Wednesday.

The first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.

The man is thought to have been in his thirties or forties, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.

Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - vessels which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.

Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.

The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight and was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.

Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people on board. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.

A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."

News.title: Olivia Dean nominated and  Lily Allen snubbed in Mercury Prize list
News.content:
Olivia Dean's campaign to collect every major music award in existence continues, with a nomination for this year's Mercury Prize.

The star is among the favourites to win the Â£25,000 prize, which recognises outstanding albums, after her second record, The Art of Loving, won album of the year at both the Brits and the Mobo Awards.

Sir Paul McCartney also receives his first ever Mercury nomination, aged 84, for the nostalgia-laden The Boys of Dungeon Lane, while Suede, Jade, Raye and Nia Archives are also in contention.

But there was a surprise omission for Lily Allen, whose scathing break-up album, West End Girl, was one of the biggest critical and commercial successes of the last 12 months.

The record examines the collapse of her marriage to actor David Harbour in unvarnished detail. Reviews praised its candour and musical invention, calling Allen's work "breathtaking and heartbreaking", external and "a brutal, tell-all masterpiece", external.

Artists submit themselves for the prize, making it impossible to determine whether Allen was snubbed or simply not in contention - but she was previously nominated for her 2018 album No Shame.

Other notable omissions include Harry Stylesâ Kiss All The Time, Disco Occasionally and Gorillazâ sweeping meditation on grief, The Mountain.

News.title: Greek police probe 'foul play' in death of woman found in suitcase
News.content:
Greek police have said they are trying to determine whether foul play was involved in the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, reportedly by a homeless man.

She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found and is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus two weeks before her death.

A spokesperson for police in Greece told the BBC: "We are awaiting the results of the toxicology tests to determine the cause of death and ascertain whether foul play was involved, as this was not clarified by the initial examination of the body."

News.title: Holidaymakers warned about 'explosive diarrhoea' cyclospora parasite infection
News.content:
UK holidaymakers are being warned about a nasty infectious disease called cyclosporiasis that can cause explosive diarrhoea, after a sharp rise in cases.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), external said 67 cases have been reported since April, with many of them among travellers returning from Mexico.

It comes amid an outbreak in the US that has infected more than 18,000 people across 45 states. The source hasn't been identified yet and there have been no reported deaths.

The illness is caused by a parasite, cyclospora, that can contaminate food like salads, herbs and soft fruits. It doesn't naturally occur in the UK and there is no risk of spread from person to person, experts stress.

Between 30 April and 15 July 2026, 30 cases have been reported in England, 27 in Scotland and 10 in Wales, according to the UKHSA.

Of the 52 cases with travel information available, 48 reported having travelled to Mexico, with many saying they had stayed in either the white sand beach resort area of Riviera Maya, or slightly north of there in coastal CancÃºn.

The UKHSA said those affected reported staying in "a range of different hotels and consuming a variety of different food and drink within their resort as part of an all-inclusive holiday package".

There are ongoing investigations and monitoring of the situation.

People can protect themselves while away by following good food and water hygiene measures, including drinking bottled water and eating thoroughly cooked food, even when staying in high-end all-inclusive resorts.

Experts also advise people avoid certain foods such as fresh uncooked berries and herbs, unpeeled fruit and salad items.

News.title: Zendaya and Tom Holland's decade-long Spider-Man romance in pictures
News.content:
Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old years old when they first met in 2016, on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the film's casting and initial production.

The film showed British actor Holland as Peter Parker balancing high school life with being a superhero - Spider-Man - for the first time.

It also introduced US actress Zendaya as MJ, his awkward but intellectual classmate.

The on-screen chemistry was clear from the start and the film received good reviews but the pair denied rumours of a romance, insisting they were just close friends while promoting the movie.

They even took to Twitter [now X] to make light of the rumours. She posted: "Wait wait ... my favourite is when it says we go on vacations together HA! I haven't been on a vacation in years! hbu @TomHolland1996 ???"

Holland responded: "Does the press tour count?"

News.title: Beauty Pie founder on how she dropped out of university and built five businesses
News.content:
Kilgore didn't always know she wanted to be an entrepreneur but growing up she saw first-hand the stress that financial insecurity could cause.

"I remember deciding at eight-years-old that when I was my parents' age, I would never want to be stressed about my electric bill," she says.

That desire shaped her approach to work and risk. "I knew that working for other people wouldn't necessarily give me the freedom I wanted and at least when you are an entrepreneur, the risk is your own."

She didn't begin with a grand business plan - she moved from Canada to New York to study at Columbia University and her tuition plan fell through so she had to get a job to support herself.

"You can't sit around thinking: 'What am I going to do? You have to survive. I knew I had to use the skills I had to support myself and then I would figure it out."

She started working as a personal trainer and taking beauty classes in the evening.

"What ended up transpiring was that I was quite good at the beauty industry job," she says and eventually she dropped out of university to pursue a career in it.

News.title: England on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates
News.content:
England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.

Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.

Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".

Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.

"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."

He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.

Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.

News.title: Mum and boyfriend jailed for girl's  murder
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A mum and her new boyfriend have been jailed for life for the "sadistic" abuse and murder of her two-year-old daughter.

Isabelle Welsh was a "happy and thriving" child before her mother, Alexandra Walker, invited Harrison Simpson into their lives in Thornaby, Stockton, in June 2025, Teesside Crown Court heard.

A judge said Isabelle was the victim of a campaign of violent and sexual abuse at the hands of those meant to love, care for and protect her.

Simpson, 22, and Walker, 26, were both found guilty of murder and child cruelty, with Simpson also convicted of sexual abuse of a child. Simpson must serve a minimum of 28 and a half years and Walker 22 years.

Ms Justice Norton said both were "equally and jointly responsible" for Isabelle's murder and the campaign of cruelty she endured, with the couple putting up a "wall of silence, lies and obfuscation" about the last weeks of her life.

News.title: Suspected Kinahan gang leader faces extradition
News.content:
Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan is to be extradited back to Ireland, BBC News NI understands.

He was arrested in Dubai under a warrant issued by the Irish courts in April but has fought attempts to extradite him.

However, his appeals have been unsuccessful and he is due to be flown back to Ireland within weeks.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) now expect authorities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to sign his extradition which will formally commence the extradition process.

GardaÃ­ expect this will take place very quickly.

Bringing the suspected gang leader back to Ireland will now be the subject of a major security operation between the gardaÃ­ and the Irish Defence Forces.

The US government imposed sanctions on him in April 2022 after he and other members of his family were identified as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.

Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton.

However, Kinahan is now expected to face the Irish courts in the coming weeks and has previously been named as the head of the drug cartel.

The Irish authorities are expected to prosecute him for his involvement in leading an organised crime group.

An extradition agreement is in place between the UAE and Ireland and it was used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the organised crime group.

He was sentenced to 24 years in prison last month for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

News.title: Jenrick urges Burnham to rule out tax rises to fund social care
News.content:
Reform UK's Robert Jenrick has urged PM Andy Burnham to rule out future tax rises to fund his plans to fix adult social care in England.

Burnham has said he wants to look at existing budgets before considering tax rises but he has not ruled them out, adding that "difficult decisions" lay ahead with funding options to be set out in a review being published next year.

Jenrick said any reforms should be paid for by cutting foreign aid and benefit payments for migrants, urging the prime minister to rule out what he called a universal "death tax".

Burnham was health secretary in a Gordon Brown government which proposed a compulsory levy which people could defer until after they had died.

The idea was labelled a "death tax" by the Conservative Party.

Burnham has not mentioned introducing an adult social care levy in this form.

He told reporters on Wednesday that proposals he put forward in 2009 were intended to stop people having to sell their home in order to pay for their care.

The new prime minister has said fixing the social care system was a top priority and he has speeded up a review of the system by Baroness Casey, which will now be published next summer.

He said the review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding that there needed to be a system in place that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

He said he would immediately start to examine, with Chancellor John Healey, how to boost the pay and training of care workers, something he said would be "fully funded" from existing budgets.

On paying for the wider shake-up of the system, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets "before we talk about tax rises".

Speaking at a press conference earlier today, Jenrick said: "He won't, he can't, he will not rule out a death tax."

The former Tory minister, who is now Reform's Treasury spokesman, called on Burnham to "rule out this tax, end the uncertainty, end the worry today".

He said he agreed with Burnham that care workers were "scandalously underpaid" and said a Reform government would stop visas for overseas workers in order to employ more British citizens.

And he said Reform would find the money to fix social care by cutting waste and raiding the foreign aid budget.

"I could not look the British taxpayer in the eye and impose a tax - another tax - before I had stopped sending taxpayers' money to rich countries overseas," he said.

The Conservatives have also called on the prime minister to rule out tax rises and further borrowing to pay for social care.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch wrote to Burnham earlier this week that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

Jenrick's speech comes a day after Burnham held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to secure cross-party support for any changes. Badenoch was unavailable.

Reform and the Green Party were not invited for talks. Both parties expressed disappointment at this.

Jenrick said he was "not surprised" Reform leader Nigel Farage had not been asked to attend.

"Andy Burnham knows that Nigel will never go along with the betrayal of people who've paid in all their lives," he said.

He insisted that Reform were serious about health and social care, despite not having a health spokesperson.

"We are absolutely at the coalface of this, trying to do our utmost to support people in difficult times. Don't tell us we don't care about this issue. We really do."

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, but it has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

News.title: ScotRail apology as passengers unable to book tickets in app launch chaos
News.content:
ScotRail has apologised for the chaotic launch of its new app, which has left hundreds of passengers unable to book train tickets.

The operator replaced its existing system, provided by Trainline, with an updated ticketing platform for travellers on Thursday morning.

Complaints on ScotRail's social media channels saw a series of issues with passengers being forced to reset account passwords and journeys not appearing in booking searches.

ScotRail said it was working to fix "intermittent technical issues" and said passengers should continue using their old phone app until resolved.

Many people attempting to catch morning trains were frustrated by the processes involved before they could buy tickets.

Passengers on social media branded the roll-out a "shambles" and a "nonsense".

News.title: Former farmer, aged 99, fulfils wish to lead cow at show one more time
News.content:
A 99-year-old care home resident in south-west Scotland has fulfilled his wish to show a cow at his local agricultural show one more time.

Staff at the Belmont Care Centre in Stranraer put a post on social media about former farmer Jackie Brown's dream in the hope of being able to see it realised.

It came to the attention of the organisers of Stranraer Show who organised for Jackie to come along to the farming event on Wednesday.

He showed one of the Ayrshire cows - just as he had done many times across his pioneering career.

News.title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss 'unable to get refunds'
News.content:
Some victims of disgraced undertaker Robert Bush have not been refunded for fake funeral plans he sold to them, a court has heard.

The 48-year-old defrauded 172 people over 11 years to the tune of Â£562,000, Hull Crown Court was told.

He previously admitted 67 offences in relation to his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, including failing to bury and cremate people, theft from 12 charities, fraudulent trading in funeral plans, and fraud.

On the fourth day of his sentencing hearing, one woman said her parents, who paid Â£2,649 each for funeral plans, were not alive "to see the justice they deserved". Another said she had not been refunded Â£5,000 for two policies.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

Wiping her eyes with a tissue, Maxine Hill told Mr Justice Hilliard the bank refused to refund the money fraudulently taken by Bush, whom she knew personally.

Bush visited both her parents, Margaret and John, in their own home and issued a handwritten receipt to her mother who paid him in cash.

The bank initially refunded the amount paid by Hill's father but 90 days later, the bank took the money back saying "there was no evidence that he hadn't received a product", the court heard.

Both have since died - Margaret in May 2024 and John in June 2025.

News.title: Virgin engineer died after traumatic brain injury
News.content:
A Virgin Atlantic engineer died after suffering a traumatic brain injury when he was hit in the face in an incident at Heathrow Airport, a coroners' court has heard.

Aircraft technician Georgie Buxton, 23, was injured on the morning of 11 June and died at St Mary's Hospital on 7 July.

Senior coroner Lydia Brown opened and suspended an inquest into his death at West London Coroners' Court on Thursday, as she is waiting to see if any criminal charges are brought.

Brown said a forensic post-mortem examination found Mr Buxton had suffered a traumatic brain injury â a craniofacial trauma.

She said: "There was an accident at Georgie's place of work. He took a trauma to the face causing him complex and tragically fatal injuries.

"He did undergo various surgeries in hospital but these were not able to save life."

Buxton started working for Virgin Atlantic two years ago, according to his LinkedIn profile, external.

Players and officials found guilty of discrimination will now face a minimum 10-game ban under enhanced Football Association rules.

This toughens previous guidelines, which recommended six to 12 games for aggravated breaches.

Such misconduct includes any express or implied reference to ethnic origin, colour, race, nationality, religion, sex, gender, gender reassignment, sexual orientation, or disability.

The new rules also apply to players, managers, and other officials.

A statement from the FA read: “The FA is committed to delivering a game free from discrimination.

“While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game.

“Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and The FA’s updated sanction guidelines will now require Regulatory Commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

Sanctions of more than 10 matches can be imposed if significant aggravating factors are present, while lesser punishments are also possible if there are mitigating factors and the individual admits the breach at the earliest opportunity.

Six matches would be the minimum ban in such cases, while the only situation in which a lesser sanction could be imposed would be if the aggravated breach took place in writing only.

Any player or official committing a second aggravated breach, meanwhile, would face a stronger sanction than for their first offence.

In June, former Watford midfielder Pierre Dwomoh was banned for 11 matches for racially abusing a team-mate.

The 22-year-old Belgian was ruled by an independent disciplinary commission to have committed “very serious” and “completely unacceptable” offences when he targeted a player of Indian heritage, who is referred to as Player A in the FA’s written reasons.

open image in gallery Dwomoh (right) was banned for 11 matches in June for racially abusing a team-mate ( Getty )

Dwomoh announced he had left the Championship club in April and his ban has been backdated to then.

The FA were keen to have his suspension increased to 16 game but this appeal was dismissed.

Watford told The Watford Observer that they support the decision to sanction Dwomoh, with The Independent understanding he was made unavailable for selection by the club as soon as the incident was self-reported.

The midfielder made one senior appearance for the Hornets last season before his exit.

Dwomoh was also fined £2,500 and ordered to complete a compulsory face-to-face education programme by 9 August.

A major incident has been declared on the Suffolk coast with properties evacuated as firefighters battle heathland blaze.

Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service have mobilised around 90 firefighters who have worked throughout the night in “arduous conditions” after the fire broke out on Wednesday afternoon on Dunwich Heath.

The “large-scale, wind-driven” inferno is currently spreading rapidly south-west, posing a threat to the 19th century St James’ Church off Westleton Road.

The fire service have evacuated residents at Coastguard Cottages, Mount Pleasant Farm and Cliff House Holiday Park, with preparations in place to evacuate 200 caravans.

Families, including babies and children, have been taken to Westleton Village Hall.

open image in gallery Around 90 firefighters have been mobilised to tackle the blaze ( Billy Rogers/Facebook )

Anna Seymour, 56, had been staying at a log cabin in Cliff House Holiday Park with her two kittens when she became aware of smoke along the heath.

"I can't remember the exact time we were [evacuated] I was sitting at the clubhouse and there was lots of noise, fire engines. It’s something you never obviously hear there because it's just not a place to hear any noise really, and lots of fire engines were going up towards the heath,” she told The Independent.

“Then it was about 20 minutes later, someone said that Dunwich was on fire. I went back to the lodge to check the kittens and then somebody knocked at the door and said, 'go to the evacuation point.'”

She described the evacuation as a calm process, but said there was a “lot of smoke” once they left the holiday site.

Justin North told the BBC that there was “hammering” on the door of his holiday cottage at Dunwich Cliffs at around 11:30pm and that he and his wife were asked to “go immediately”.

open image in gallery Firefighters are set to continue dealing with the blaze for the next 24 to 48 hours ( Sky News )

The couple had to sleep in their car before being able to access the evacuation centre, where they said there was a “kind of blitz spirit” among the residents.

There is no current risk to Sizewell B, a nuclear power station which provides electricity to 2.5 million households, due to the distance of the fire, but firefighters warn it is a “live and dynamic situation”.

An EDF spokesperson said: "The fire at Dunwich Heath is not currently affecting operations at Sizewell B power station but we are continuing to monitor the situation."

It comes as the UK experiences its second drought in two years as very low rainfall and high temperatures take a toll on the environment, affecting 28 million people.

The Environment Agency warned that swathes of England are suffering from “flash drought”, including East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex – covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and Gloucestershire.

open image in gallery Fire service crews have made preparations to evacuate 200 caravans ( Billy Rogers/Facebook )

Authorities confirmed the major incident status was enacted in Suffolk "due to the size and complexity" of the rapidly developing situation.

Dan Davis, a station manager for the service, has issued an urgent plea for the public to steer clear of the area and ensure windows and doors remain shut.

The fire service requested that people avoided visiting Dunwich Beach, adding: “We understand that the warm weather makes a trip to the coast very appealing, but for everyone's safety we are asking people to stay away from the area at this time.”

Thérèse Coffey, the former Tory MP for the area, said it was “sad news” and expressed hope that the blaze did not spread to the RSPB Minsmere nature reserve.

It comes amid UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) issuing an amber heat-health alert for the East Midlands, the East, South East and London.

open image in gallery Firefighters are still working to contain a wildfire in the Cairngorms that broke out two weeks ago ( Getty )

The alert remains in place until 9am on Thursday, with the agency previously warning that rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

The Suffolk blaze is one of several major wildfires being tackled across the UK.

Fire services in England and Wales have so far responded to 706 wildfires in 2026, with more than 200 recorded in the last two weeks, the National Fire Chiefs Council said.

Eight wildfires are currently burning and “being monitored” across the UK, with fire chiefs warning that there remains an “elevated risk” of more igniting.

Separately, in Scotland, crews said they were making “significant progress” tackling a wildfire in the Cairngorms that broke out two weeks ago.

A number of homes in the remote region were evacuated as plumes of smoke billowed into the sky, and vast swathes of trees, heather and grasslands have been left charred and blackened.

Speaking on the track on Wednesday, Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) deputy assistant chief officer Michael Humphreys said that fire crews are making progress in tackling the blaze.

However, he warned the risk of flare-ups remains high.

“It’s been an absolutely devastating fire for wildlife and for the local community who have come out in force to really support us, which we really do appreciate,” he said.

“To control this fire, what we’ve had to put in place is a significant number of fire breaks.”

President Donald Trump is “exasperated” by the lack of progress in ending the Iran conflict and the lack of consensus on strategy among his top military advisers, according to a report.

An unnamed ally of the president has told NBC News: “The president is exasperated. I don’t think he believed it was going to be this difficult to get the Iranians to agree to a deal.

“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint… He did not intend this to be a long, drawn-out war.”

A U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that the root of Trump’s frustrations lay in the lack of agreement about how to proceed with a war that began with joint U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on February 28 that killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei but quickly brought retaliation, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and, ultimately, stalemate.

“After all this time, there is no unity,” the official said. “We have had a series of tactical victories but are facing a strategic defeat without clear policy guidance or a decision about where this is going.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump is reportedly growing ‘exasperated’ over the failure to conclude the Iran war he started in February ( AP )

The source told NBC that Trump had “erupted” during a meeting with his top national security team last week and had even yelled expletives at those present.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt has denied that the incident took place, however, telling NBC: “This is false. The president has a great team whom he trusts, and everyone on the team knows he’s the final decision-maker.”

Leavitt subsequently told The Independent that the president “is not going to stand by as they break the [memorandum of understanding], kill our soldiers and fire at our ships in the Strait.

“So until that behavior changes, his behavior will not change. He’s locked and loaded to keep punishing Iran.”

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell likewise said the Department of Defense was “locked and loaded, ready to execute the president’s directives at a moment’s notice.”

open image in gallery Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is said to back the further use of military force against Tehran, but others in the administration are not convinced ( Reuters )

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine “stand completely aligned and are united in mission, strategy, and resolve regarding overseas operations involving Iran,” Parnell added.

The Independent also reached out to the Pentagon for further comment.

Trump promised during his 2024 presidential campaign that he would not lead the U.S. into any further “forever war” commitments overseas, only to follow his Operation Midnight Hammer strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities last summer with another conflict that he once described as a “short-term excursion” but which is about to enter its sixth month.

Despite the president’s repeated insistence that Tehran is “desperate” to make a deal to end the hostilities, it has proven itself a tough negotiator and has not shied away from launching fresh attacks of its own.

Meanwhile, on the domestic front, many of Trump’s fellow Republicans are keen to draw a line under an unpopular war in good time for November’s midterms.

open image in gallery Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains an influential voice on Iran and was in Washington this week to attend the funeral of South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham ( Reuters )

They remain fearful that its impact on gas prices could count against GOP candidates at the ballot box, who could bear the brunt of a protest vote that threatens to sweep the Democrats back to power in Congress.

The president has remained characteristically bullish, however, telling Fox News Wednesday: “We are going to beat the f***ing s*** out of them… We’ll be hitting them hard. They are going to get a beating.”

He also expressed perplexity about Iran’s attitude towards diplomacy following the failure of the MOU signed in Versailles in June, commenting: “For some reason, we can be in the midst of a beautiful discussion, and they’ll come out and say ‘we’re not talking.’”

According to NBC, the difference of opinion within Trump’s camp can be broadly divided into two factions: Hegseth and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu back the use of greater military force against Iran – although the latter is not thought to have raised prospect with the president when they met in Washington this week – while Vice President JD Vance and Caine question what that would achieve.

The chairman of the joint chiefs, for one, is said to have advised Trump against allowing the continued depletion of U.S. munitions stockpiles through prolonged strikes.

News.title: Uefa debate World Cup boycott at emergency meeting after Gianni Infantino bombshell - latest
News.content:
Fifa's World Cup plan is worse than the Super League

Uefa will discuss boycotting the World Cup in response to Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell of stakes in Fifa’s major tournaments to external investors, including members of Donald Trump’s family.

The governing body of European football has led the furious response to Infantino’s proposals and called an emergency meeting to discuss how to they can leverage their position. That includes the threat of boycotting the tournament, as a World Cup without major nations such as champions Spain, France, Germany and England would be hugely damaging to Infantino.

Uefa were left dismayed that Infantino has given Fifa’s member associations just 53 days to decide their position and were outraged by Infantino promising a $40m (£30m) windfall to nations who back the proposals, or have the one-off payment withdrawn. “This says everything you need to know about this plan,” Uefa said in a statement on Wednesday.

Uefa, which previously said that Infantino’s plans “crossed a line”, will hold their emergency meeting with its 55 member associations virtually and knows it will require support from another confederation to block Infantino’s plans. Meanwhile, the head of the Czech FA backed Fifa’s proposals on Wednesday, which suggests Infantino carries some support within Europe as well.

Matthias Jaissle is in pole position to replace Eddie Howe as Newcastle manager – just three weeks out from the new Premier League season.

Howe is leaving his role as Magpies head coach after five years in charge, with the 48-year-old English coach keen to take a break from football. Newcastle lost 4-1 to Bristol City in a pre-season game on Wednesday.

Howe leaves with plenty of credit in the bank, having guided Newcastle to their first major trophy in 70 years with victory in the 2025 Carabao Cup. He also guided the North-East side to the last-16 of the Champions League last season.

Yet, as first broken in The Athletic, Howe looks set to be replaced by little-known German coach Jaissle, who will have to hit the ground running with just 24 days before their Premier League opener against Liverpool at St James’ Park.

Here’s everything you need to know about Matthias Jaissle.

Who is Matthias Jaissle?

The 38-year-old German coach is a two-time Asian Champions League winner with Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli – a club majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), just like Newcastle.

Jaissle has coached Al-Ahli – who boast players such as Ivan Toney and Edouard Mendy – since 2023 and also won the Saudi Super Cup in 2025.

Prior to that, he coached Red Bull Salzburg for two seasons, winning consecutive Austrian Bundesliga titles and the Austrian Cup after succeeding ex-Leeds boss Jesse Marsch. He also led Salzburg to the Champions League knockout phase.

Jaissle obtained the job at Salzburg just four months after guiding Liefering to second place in the second tier of Austrian football. That being said, he was previously manager of Red Bull Salzburg’s Under-18 academy team.

open image in gallery Jaissle, 38, has coached Al Ahli since 2023 ( Getty )

Jaissle had a modest playing career, featuring for Hoffenheim as a centre-back for seven years but making only 68 league appearances after an ACL tear in 2009 triggered his retirement at 25. He also earned one cap for Germany’s Under-21 side

The German started his career in the youth teams at VfB Stuttgart, where he was coached by Thomas Tuchel, with whom he has a close friendship. Many believe this relationship was key in Toney being called up to England’s World Cup squad.

He has a coaching philosophy of high-intensity, attacking football and, given he started out in the Red Bull ecosystem, sees ex-Man United manager Ralf Rangnick as a source of inspiration.

“I want stress on the opponent as soon as possible,” he said in an interview in January. “And when we win the ball, I want to go as quickly as possible towards the opponent’s goal.

“I’m very vertical in that approach.”

Why have Newcastle appointed him?

The clear link is that PIF own both Newcastle and Al Ahli.

However, Jaissle has built a strong reputation as one of the world’s top young coaches, having won trophies and achieved success wherever he has gone. His time at RB Salzburg was particularly impressive, before he ventured to Saudi Arabia and became the first-ever coach to win back-to-back Asian Champions League titles.

However, it is quite the shift from Newcastle’s last three coaches, who have all been English: Howe, Graeme Jones (interim) and Steve Bruce.

In fact, it is the first time in Newcastle’s history that they have appointed a German manager – and it’s just their third non-British/Irish coach.

Newcastle are next in action on Saturday 8 August in a friendly against Valencia, before their final warm-up games of the season against Everton, Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg.

News.title: The Latest: US and Iran trade strikes as hopes dim for a quick resolution
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

The U.S. and Iran each fired barrages of missiles Thursday, as the pattern of back-and-forth strikes took hold again and hope dimmed for any quick resolution. After a brief respite, the risk of a return to all-out war emerged once more, with the fighting threatening to engulf even more countries. Jordan said Thursday it intercepted Iranian missiles for the second consecutive day, while Kuwait said a strike in the northern part of the country killed one person.

Todd Blanche’s nomination to become attorney general stalled Wednesday as lawmakers scrapped a planned committee vote after key Republicans demanded more assurances about the settlement of President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, and Trump’s approval rating on Iran has fallen slightly since last month, according to a new AP-NORC poll. The results are a stark repudiation of Trump’s approach to the conflict, which has dragged on far longer than he originally predicted.

Here's the Latest:

Opposition to FIFA’s World Cup private equity plan grows

Global opposition is growing to FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s plan for selling a stake in World Cup revenue to private investors.

The FIFA project would be underwritten by a New York investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. Infantino has had close ties to Jared Kushner and held secret talks with potential backers the U.S. about creating the $20 billion FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary with $4.2 billion of private equity.

“FIFA’s unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football,” the Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa warned in a letter Thursday to member federations that was seen by The Associated Press.

It circulated as the 55-nation European soccer body UEFA prepared meet Thursday to shape a resistance strategy. The 35-member North American soccer body CONCACAF, meanwhile, said it is “deeply concerned by the lack of due process” in Infantino’s project.

▶ Read more

US economy turns in sluggish 1.5% second-quarter growth and inflation remains above Fed target

The U.S. economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5% pace from April through June as rising imports weighed on growth. But consumer spending rose. And the Federal Reserve’s favored measure of inflation grew more slowly last month, by 3.7%, but remained above the central bank’s 2% target.

The Commerce Department reported Thursday that growth in U.S. gross domestic product — the nation’s output of goods and services — decelerated from 2.1% in the first three months of 2026 and came in below economists’ expectations.

The Fed on Wednesday chose to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the fifth straight meeting. But three regional Fed presidents dissented, saying they wanted to raise rates to combat elevated inflation.

Higher costs have frustrated Americans ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump’s Republicans keep full control of Congress.

US filings for jobless benefits rise to 197,000 last week, but layoffs remain historically low

The number of Americans applying for unemployment benefits rose last week but layoffs remain in the historically healthy range of the past few years.

U.S. filings for jobless aid in the week ending July 25 rose by 9,000 to 197,000, the Labor Department reported Thursday. The previous week’s figure was revised up by 1,000 to 188,000 but remains the lowest in more than 50 years.

Analysts surveyed by the data firm FactSet forecast 207,000 new applications.

Weekly filings for unemployment benefits are considered representative of layoffs and are close to a real-time indicator of the health of the U.S. job market.

Urban League report says Trump harms Black Americans’ chances at American Dream

The American Dream may not be dead for many Black Americans, but a National Urban League report warns that it’s further away than at any point since the Civil Rights Movement.

The 50th annual “State of Black America” report released Thursday grimly describes Black Americans ’ economic and political prospects as having worsened due to Trump’s policies. A copy obtained by The Associated Press says all Americans should be concerned.

“While they have targeted and focused on Black Americans, these attacks are going to impact broadly working Americans, poor Americans, aspirational middle-class Americans, and this is what this report points to,” said Marc Morial, the league’s president and CEO.

Morial urged concerned Americans to respond at the ballot box and with their pocketbooks. “We cannot be dejected. We cannot be cynical. We must act,” Morial said.

▶ Read more

Most say it’s important to keep gas prices down: AP-NORC poll

Many Americans continue to be concerned about the pocketbook impact of the Iran war, the new poll shows.

About 7 in 10 U.S. adults — 72% — say it’s “extremely” or “very” important for the U.S. to prevent domestic oil and gas prices from rising, up slightly from 67% in March.

A similar share, 70%, say it’s highly important for the U.S. to reach a ceasefire agreement with Iran.

Americans’ goals for the Iran war may not be fully aligned with Trump, who has repeatedly said the war was launched to keep a nuclear weapon out of Iran’s hands.

While about two-thirds of U.S. adults say it’s “extremely” or “very” important to keep Iran from gaining a nuclear weapon — with Republicans especially likely to say this — Americans are more likely to prioritize low gas prices and a permanent ceasefire with Iran.

About two-thirds say the Iran war is not worth fighting: AP-NORC poll

Most U.S. adults say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, according to a new AP-NORC poll. About two-thirds of U.S. adults say the war with Iran, which began Feb. 28, has not been worthwhile. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as about 37% Republicans.

The poll shows little appetite among Americans for a prolonged conflict.

Only about 2 in 10 U.S. adults want to continue military action in Iran, while about 3 in 10 say the U.S. should pause military action and seek a renewed ceasefire through negotiations. About 2 in 10 want to completely stop military action in Iran and roughly one-quarter don’t know enough to say.

Trump announces a $22.5B makeover of Dulles airport that will eliminate the ‘people movers’

Trump on Wednesday announced a $22.5 billion renovation of Washington Dulles International Airport that will end the use of the widely disliked “people movers,” the mobile lounges that have been used for decades to shuttle travelers to and from the main terminal.

In place of the people movers, the airport will add a new U-shaped passenger train, a central walking tunnel, more moving walkways and new concourses. An above-ground parking garage closer to the main terminal with space for 32,000 vehicles is also in the offing, according to Trump and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

The airport makeover would add to a long list of renovation projects the Republican president is pursuing to leave a lasting mark on the Washington region after his term ends in January 2029. Among other undertakings, he is building a new White House ballroom and wants to build a towering triumphal arch near the Lincoln Memorial.

▶ Read more

Trump’s approval rating for handling of Iran has declined slightly: AP-NORC poll

The president's approval rating on Iran has fallen slightly since last month, according to a new AP-NORC poll.

Just 28% of U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling Iran, a slight decline from 34% last month.

Republicans also appear to be increasingly unhappy with the prolonged conflict: 61% approve of how Trump is handling Iran, an apparent decline from 71% in June.

The margin of sampling error for Republicans is 6 points, so that 10-point decline is considered slight – but it’s still noteworthy given Republicans’ higher approval of how Trump is handling the presidency overall. About 7 in 10 Republicans, 73%, approve of Trump’s job performance.

Trump’s overall job approval rating is 33% among U.S. adults. That’s slightly below where he was at this point in his first term, and similar to where former President Biden stood about one and a half years into his presidency, as inflation peaked.

Senate panel delays vote on Blanche attorney general nomination as key Republicans withhold support

Todd Blanche’s nomination to become attorney general stalled Wednesday as lawmakers scrapped a planned committee vote after key Republicans demanded more assurances about the settlement of President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

The Senate Judiciary Committee had been expected to vote Thursday on whether to advance Blanche’s nomination to the full chamber. But resistance from two Republican senators on the committee who could block Blanche’s nomination threw his confirmation into doubt.

A spokesperson for the committee said in a statement Wednesday night that the vote would be postponed “as work continues to secure sufficient support.” The delay came after hours of negotiations between the Justice Department and Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis over the controversial settlement that afforded Trump and members of his family protection from tax audits.
