Eleven years after the apps arrived, Costa Rica still has not decided what they legally are.

World.title: Costa Rica Wins Its First Surfing Gold Medal in Regional Games History
World.content:
Costa Rican surfer Rachel Agüero Cabezas won the women’s shortboard title at the Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic tpday, delivering Costa Rica its first gold medal in surfing in the history of the regional competition.

The 20-year-old beat Barbados’ Chelsea Tuach 10.50 points to 7.33 in the final at Playa Encuentro in Cabarete, on the northern coast of Puerto Plata province. Agüero’s score came from two waves graded 5.83 and 4.67, while Tuach posted a 5.00 and a 2.33. According to the National Olympic Committee, Agüero took control of the heat from the opening minutes and never surrendered the lead. Tuach needed a wave scored at 5.51 or better to overturn the result and never found one.

Agüero reached the final by eliminating the surfer most observers had installed as the favorite. In the fourth round she defeated Nicaragua’s Candelaria Resano, an Olympian and world championship medalist, by 12.57 points to 11.33. She had opened the competition on the first day of the event with 11.16 points, built on waves of 7.33 and 3.83, to win her heat ahead of Puerto Rico’s Havanna Cabrero and Colombia’s Margarita Conde. That 7.33 stood as the highest-scoring women’s wave of the opening day.

The result caps a season that has established Agüero as the leading woman in Costa Rican competitive surfing. She arrived in the Dominican Republic as the two-time national Open champion, having sealed her second consecutive title only weeks earlier at the closing round of the Banco LAFISE national circuit at Playa Hermosa de Jacó, the beach where she lives and trains.

In March she won the Denga Santa Teresa Pro at Playa Carmen. She has also been competing on World Surf League regional events, the tier where surfers accumulate the results and ranking points that open the door to the sport’s professional circuits. Costa Rica had never won a surfing gold medal at these Games before Wednesday. The country’s only previous podium finishes in the sport came at San Salvador 2023, when Lía Díaz and Anthony Flores each took bronze in longboard.

Sam Reidy added another on Tuesday, beating the Dominican Republic’s Gian Marco Oliva 14.50 to 11.60 in the men’s shortboard bronze heat, a result the Costa Rican Surf Federation described as the first shortboard medal at the Games. Flores finished fourth in the men’s longboard event this year after losing his bronze heat to Mexico’s Heriberto Torres.

The surfing competition ran from July 25 until today at Playa Encuentro, a break that has become one of the Caribbean’s most reliable competitive venues, and drew 71 surfers from 12 countries across shortboard, longboard and stand-up paddle surf. Agüero’s medal was Costa Rica’s third gold of Santo Domingo 2026. The first two came in taekwondo, through Jaycee Bassett and Neshy Lindo.

This edition of the Games is the 25th and marks a century since the first was held in Mexico City in 1926. Organizers programmed 40 sports, more than the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic schedule, and more than 6,200 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing over 16 days.

Costa Rican surfing has been producing this kind of result with increasing regularity. Díaz became the first surfer from Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America to qualify for the World Surf League’s Longboard Tour, a circuit that opened its season at Huntington Beach in California this month.

Leilani McGonagle won a place on the 2026-27 Challenger Series, the qualifying tier immediately below the elite Championship Tour. Bodyboarder Dulce Agüero reached a podium at Pipeline in Hawaii in March. The national federation has said its planning is now oriented around the qualifying events for the 2028 Olympics, where surfing will again be on the program.

For Agüero, the initial reward is a regional title at 20 and a clear line of sight to the next stage. The Pan American Games in Lima in 2027 come first, and the Olympic qualifying calendar follows behind it.

World.title: Costa Rica Expels Second-Division Club for 10 Years Over Match-Fixing
World.content:
The Costa Rican Football Federation has thrown a second-division club out of the sport for ten years after its investigators concluded the team took part in manipulating four matches during the 2025 season, in what is now the fifth match-fixing case in Costa Rican football to end in sanctions.

The Disciplinary Commission of the Federación Costarricense de Fútbol found that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, which competed in the Liga de Ascenso under the name San Carlos FC, breached Article 66 of the federation’s Disciplinary Code. The resolution bars the club from any football-related activity for a decade. The federation’s legal department has since notified every affiliated league — the first division, the Liga de Ascenso, the amateur Linafa structure, futsal, beach football and women’s football — that the prohibition applies to the legal entity regardless of category or format.

The case rests on a report by the federation’s Integrity Office, led by Carlos Ricardo Benavides, which examined four Liga de Ascenso fixtures from the 2024-2025 season. All four ended in lopsided defeats. San Carlos FC lost 8-2 to Quepos Cambute on January 19, 2025, fell 5-1 to Cofutpa on February 9, lost 6-2 away to Municipal Grecia on March 1, and lost 5-2 to Jicaral on March 9. According to the resolution, the investigation found a sustained pattern of irregularities in sports betting linked to matches the club played, together with atypical movement in betting markets.

Much of that evidence came from outside Costa Rica. Sportradar, the sports data firm that assists FIFA with integrity investigations, issued alerts on several of the club’s fixtures after analysing both the state of betting markets before kickoff and the swings recorded while games were in progress. In the Quepos Cambute match, San Carlos FC was leading 1-0 at the 27th minute when heavy money began moving on a San Carlos defeat; the game finished 8-2 to Quepos Cambute.

Sportradar filed a report flagging irregular movement five days later, on January 24. Investigators also drew on reports from the bookmakers Betway, VBet and 9 Olybet and from the International Betting Integrity Association. The Integrity Office concluded that the relationship between the market swings and what happened on the pitch pointed to a high probability of deliberate intervention by the club.

The commission’s finding, as set out in the resolution, is that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, known as San Carlos FC, played an active part in the conduct. The franchise had been based in the Pacific canton of Garabito before its owners moved the operation north; the club then competed as San Carlos FC in the Northern Zone. It was relegated from the Liga de Ascenso at the end of the 2024-2025 season and did not subsequently compete in Linafa. The club has no connection to AD San Carlos of the first division, nor to Inter San Carlos, which recently won the Liga de Ascenso title.

Three players who turned out for the club were sanctioned in a separate resolution that became final on June 25 of this year. That file concerned an approach made in April 2025 to players at Deportivo Upala, who were offered money to lose a Liga de Ascenso fixture against San Carlos FC.

The attempt failed because the Upala players reported it. Hansell Arauz Ovares, a retired forward who won four national titles with Deportivo Saprissa between 2014 and 2016, and Henry Cooper Bennett, a former Limón FC striker, were each banned for 15 years. Goalkeeper Fabián Rodríguez Esquivel received 15 years in the same file and a further 20 years in a separate case in which the Integrity Office concluded he had approached a Guadalupe FC player about fixing a first-division match, bringing his total ban to 35 years. All three bans cover any football-related role, whether as a player, coaching staff or club official.

The club expulsion is the second of its kind in Costa Rica. Puerto Golfito FC was excluded for ten years in 2024 on similar grounds. In 2025, three Municipal Turrialba officials — Enrique Valencia, Ernesto de la Torre and Rolando Pereira — were suspended for five years over an alleged manipulation attempt. Each of the cases sanctioned so far has originated in the lower tiers of the Costa Rican game, where budgets are thin, wages are low and matches still attract enough betting volume abroad to make manipulation worth someone’s while.

In notifying every affiliated league of the expulsion, the federation asked each to apply its integrity protocols and strengthen preventive measures. The Integrity Office has indicated that further resolutions are pending.

World.title: Trump’s Granddaughter Puts Guanacaste Beach Town in Front of 1.5 Million Viewers
World.content:
A travel vlog posted last week by Kai Trump, the eldest granddaughter of U.S. President Donald Trump, has put a small stretch of Guanacaste coastline in front of one of the largest young American audiences any Costa Rican destination has reached this year.

The 19-year-old published the video to her YouTube channel on July 25, where it went out to more than 1.5 million subscribers. She framed the trip as a send-off with high school friends before the group scatters to university, with Trump herself starting at the University of Miami this fall.

The footage moves through the familiar sequence of a Guanacaste beach holiday — mornings at the hotel pool, a climb to a ridgeline lookout, boogie boarding in the surf, ice cream, long outdoor dinners, card games, and a sunset she describes as spectacular. At one point she tells the camera she never wants to leave and would move to Costa Rica.

According to records from the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería, Trump was here from June 11 to June 14 and stayed at a hotel in Playa Las Catalinas, in the area of Santa Cruz, Guanacaste. That places the visit roughly six weeks before the video reached the public, a gap that is standard practice for creators who edit and stage travel content for release when it will draw the most attention.

Las Catalinas is an unusual setting for this kind of exposure. Founded in 2006 on a previously undeveloped stretch of Pacific coast, the planned town covers about 485 hectares (1,200 acres) and was laid out on car-free, fully walkable principles, with plazas arranged around Playa Danta and a network of trails climbing into the dry forest behind it.

It sits roughly an hour by road from Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia, which is what allows a four-day trip of this kind to work at all. The development has spent close to two decades positioning itself toward exactly the high-spending, design-conscious North American traveler the vlog’s audience will grow into.

The video did not travel cleanly. Within days of release, U.S. and British outlets seized on the contrast between the trip and domestic economic sentiment, citing polling that found the overwhelming majority of Americans surveyed believe Costa Rica is in an affordability crisis. Commenters on the video and on aggregated coverage split between praise for the destination and criticism of the timing. Trump has faced similar reaction before, including over a grocery-shopping video posted in March, and has said publicly that the criticism does not affect her.

None of that argument is about Costa Rica, and the destination itself came through the coverage largely untouched. Costa Rica has become a recurring stop for the family — Trump’s aunt, Ivanka Trump, spent Passover and Easter week here in 2025 with her husband and children, drawing a similar mix of enthusiasm and criticism at the time. Trump has said on her own channels that Costa Rica ranks among her favorite places to travel, and she has a long-standing friendship with a Costa Rican classmate that predates the trip.

What the episode illustrates is how little control a destination has over the terms on which it gets seen. Guanacaste’s tourism spends heavily to reach American travelers in their twenties and thirties, a demographic that increasingly makes destination decisions from short-form video rather than from advertising. A four-day trip in June, edited and released in late July by someone with a national profile, delivered that reach in a single upload — bundled together with a political argument Costa Rica had no part in and no ability to steer.

World.title: Ride-app protest could slow your drive across the Valle Central this morning
World.content:
If you have a flight out of Juan Santamaría today, a shuttle booked to the airport, or a drive between Cartago and San José, leave earlier than you planned. Ride-app drivers have called a protest for 9 a.m. today, and the roads they say they will use are the ones that carry nearly everyone.

Organizers say the convoy will roll along Ruta 1 in Alajuela, through Ochomogo, past Sabanilla and onto Circunvalación, finishing at Casa Presidencial in Zapote. Those details come from the drivers themselves. As of first light Wednesday, the Policía de Tránsito had not published an advisory confirming the route, so treat that list as the plan rather than the result. Plans like this one shift, shrink or start late.

What the drivers have called is a tortuguismo, a go-slow. Nobody blocks anything. The convoy simply travels in a pack at a crawl, and every vehicle behind it travels at the same speed. That distinction is the whole story for you. A closure gets you a detour, an officer waving you around, and a police post you can see from a distance. A go-slow gets you none of that. There is no sign, no announcement, and no way to tell you are in it until you already are. Once you are boxed in on a divided highway, your only real option is to wait.

Ruta 1 is the reason this matters to travelers. It is the corridor between San José and Juan Santamaría, so anything that slows it slows every airport transfer, every hotel shuttle and every rental car heading for a return desk. Ochomogo sits on the climb between Cartago and San José and is the pinch point for that whole side of the valley. Circunvalación is the ring road that absorbs traffic coming off Ruta 27 and feeds it around the capital toward Zapote. Between them, those three points decide whether the Valle Central moves.

If you are flying out this morning and have not left yet, go now. Whatever cushion you would normally give yourself, add an hour on top of it. That sounds excessive on a normal Wednesday, and on a normal Wednesday it would be. The problem with a go-slow is that the delay is not proportional to the protest.

A few dozen vehicles moving at 20 kilometers per hour (about 12 miles per hour) for half an hour can leave a line that takes two hours to drain, because the road behind them keeps filling at normal speed while the front of it empties at a crawl. You do not lose the time the protest lasts. You lose the time it takes the backlog to clear.

Check in online before you leave, and if you have a bag to drop, know your airline’s cutoff rather than guessing at it. If you are running late, call the airline from the road rather than waiting until you reach the counter. Missing a bag cutoff by ten minutes is a different problem than missing a flight, and airlines can sometimes do something about the first if they hear from you early.

If you are already on Ruta 1 and traffic ahead of you dies, stay in the lane you are in. Weaving between lanes to get past a convoy does not work, and on that stretch it puts you alongside heavy trucks that cannot stop quickly. Do not try to overtake the group. If you have not yet committed to the highway, Ruta 3, the old road through Heredia and Alajuela, runs roughly parallel and gives you a way to reach the airport without joining the line. It is slower on a good day and it will be crowded today, but a slow road that is moving beats a fast road that is not.

Coming from Cartago, the alternative to Florencio del Castillo is the old road, and this week that carries a complication of its own. The Romería is already underway. Tránsito started its operation on July 25 with about 150 officers on that corridor and reinforces it between July 31 and August 2, and pilgrims are walking the shoulder in numbers. The old road is an option this morning, but drive it expecting people on foot rather than a clear run.

If you are not traveling and have nothing that cannot move, the simplest answer is to not drive between roughly 9 a.m. and midday. Reschedule the Zapote appointment. Take the errand in the afternoon. Every vehicle that stays home is one that is not in the line in front of somebody trying to catch a plane.

Behind all of this is a bill that has been moving through the Legislative Assembly for years. Expediente 23.736 would regulate transport offered through platforms such as Uber and DiDi, requiring drivers to register with the CCSS and Hacienda, pay an annual permit, and meet insurance and background requirements. The Comisión de Gobierno y Administración finished working through 282 mociones de fondo on Tuesday and approved nine of them, sending the revised text back to the plenary. That vote is what put drivers on the road this morning.

The drivers want two things added before it passes. They want a ceiling on the commission platforms take from each fare, and they want guaranteed benefits and due process when a company deactivates an account. Drivers made both demands at the Assembly earlier this month, saying they had not been heard during the drafting.

Aprimotec, an association representing platform drivers, asked the Assembly and the Executive on July 20 to stop the bill’s advance altogether, arguing the text was written around the traditional taxi sector and would push drivers out of the work rather than formalize it. The taxi sector sees it differently. Canatrans, Fenacotaxi, the Foro Nacional de Taxistas and other transport groups have publicly backed the bill, framing it as legal certainty and fair competition.

Neither side is likely to settle it this morning. What will be settled by lunchtime is whether you made your flight.

World.title: ‘BAD FREAK’ CHARGED ON STEAMY WEDNESDAY; ‘WAR RIOR’ ON THE RUN – WHO WON THE FIGHT?
World.content:
‘BAD FREAK’ CHARGED ON STEAMY WEDNESDAY; ‘WAR RIOR’ ON THE RUN – WHO WON THE FIGHT?

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A viral Facebook fight between two Belize City women known on social media as “Bad Freak” and “War Rior” has resulted in a disorderly conduct charge, with one woman fined and the other still being sought by police.

Twenty-two-year-old Britney Nichole Daly, also known as “Bad Freak,” appeared in Court #3 at the Belize City Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, July 29, where she pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct.

The charge arose from a public fight on Freedom Street on Tuesday, July 28, involving Daly and Shala Smith, also known as “War Rior.” Video of the altercation quickly circulated on social media.

Police reportedly arrived after the fight had ended and those involved had already dispersed. Authorities later used footage from the Police Fusion Centre’s surveillance cameras to identify the women, leading to Daly’s detention.

Daly, a musician who resides at #22 Freedom Street, was fined $150 plus $5 in court costs. She has until September 30, 2026, to pay the total, or she will face one month in prison.

Outside the courthouse, Daly was asked what prompted the fight.

“To prove a point,” she replied before entering a waiting taxi.

Police say Smith remains at large and is being sought for the same charge of disorderly conduct.

World.title: Man charged and fined $1,000 for molesting wild jaguar cub
World.content:
Man charged and fined $1,000 for molesting wild jaguar cub

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The case of the wild jaguar cub handled in the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve has reached its legal conclusion. The Belize Forest Department has announced that Ruben Stoll was charged under the Wildlife Protection Act in connection with the incident, and has paid a fine of BZ$1,000, approximately US$500.

According to the department’s official statement issued from Belmopan on July 29, 2026, Stoll was charged under the Wildlife Protection Act, Chapter 220 of the Laws of Belize, in connection with the incident involving the handling and molestation of a wild jaguar cub within the reserve.

Following the incident, the department stated, Stoll voluntarily returned to Belize and surrendered himself to the authorities, indicating he had been outside the country. He was subsequently charged and paid the fine.

The department paired the announcement with an unambiguous message to the public. Wildlife, it stressed, is not to be treated as pets, photo props, or tourist attractions, and approaching, touching, handling, or otherwise disturbing wild animals can place both people and wildlife at serious risk.

The legal foundation is broad by design. The jaguar is one of Belize’s protected species, and the Wildlife Protection Act defines “to hunt” as “to kill, take, or molest by any method and includes attempting to kill, take, or molest by any method any species of wildlife,” prohibiting the hunting of protected wildlife, obviously immature wildlife, and any female accompanied by its young. A cub, in other words, is covered several times over.

“No one is above the laws of Belize,” the department declared, reminding Belizeans and visitors alike that while the country welcomes the world to enjoy its extraordinary biodiversity, everyone bears responsibility to respect its wildlife, protected areas, and laws.

The resolution will nonetheless leave some Belizeans weighing the arithmetic: a thousand dollars for the molestation of a protected jaguar cub, the national animal’s most vulnerable form, is a figure the public conversation may judge against the offence. The penalty applied is the penalty the law provides, and any change to it belongs to lawmakers.

The department’s closing guidance is the piece worth carrying forward, for every trail, reserve, and encounter: observe wildlife from a safe distance. Admire it. Photograph it. But never touch it, harass it, or interfere with it.

World.title: Wingz Police battle B-Town Savage Storm in Friday’s Big 6K Match
World.content:
Wingz Police battle B-Town Savage Storm in Friday’s Big 6K Match

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belmopan, clear your Friday. July 31 brings the Big 6K Match to the FFB Stadium, and when the final whistle blows, the night is only getting started.

The football comes in doubles. The 6K Qualifier kicks things off at 7:30 p.m. with a north versus west clash, Progresso FC Amateur out of the north taking on Benque Power from the western border. Then the main event at 9:30 p.m.: Wingz Police, backed by Wingz Belmopan, against B-Town Savage Storm in the Big 6K Match, sanctioned under the Football Federation of Belize and presented by Play Chune Marketing.

And when the stadium empties, the city lights up. Three clubs, three afta parties, one Friday night. La Cabana runs with Cloud 9, Dalla, Movements and Absoh. MJ’s Dragon brings Eclipse, Fyah Statah and Freezy. Glow Lounge stacks DJ Sambo and DJ Smallz, Wakky, Cinimax and DJ Rhyno.

Whatever your vibe, there is a dance floor with your name on it, and the hardest decision of the night will not be made at the stadium.

Friday, July 31. FFB Stadium, Belmopan. Come for the ball, stay for everything after.

World.title: Minister of Economic Transformation and delegation meet Belizean students in Taiwan
World.content:
Minister of Economic Transformation and delegation meet Belizean students in Taiwan

By Zoila Palma: Today, Osmond Martinez, Minister of State in the Ministry of Economic Transformation, and his delegation met with Belizean students in Taiwan.

The students shared their experiences and perspectives on their studies, culture, and life in Taiwan.

Minister Martinez emphasized that studying in Taiwan contributes to Belize’s human capital development by exposing students to advanced training and real-world innovation in areas where the country needs deeper expertise, particularly information technology, international relations, public health, and border security.

Minister Martinez and his delegation are visiting Taiwan from July 27 to 31, 2026.

World.title: Institute for Social and Cultural Research discuss safeguarding living traditions of Deer Dance
World.content:
Institute for Social and Cultural Research discuss safeguarding living traditions of Deer Dance

By Zoila Palma: On July 24, 2026, the Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) and cultural advocates from the communities of Armenia, Maya Mopan, and Valley of Peace met to discuss the ongoing efforts to safeguard the living traditions of the Deer Dance.

Led by ISCR Director Rolando Cocom, the engagement provided an opportunity for community practitioners to share their knowledge, reaffirm the importance of honouring cultural traditions and community protocols, and identify meaningful pathways for continued collaboration in safeguarding this cherished heritage.

Looking ahead, ISCR will extend consultations to Deer Dance practitioners from communities in southern Belize. Through continued dialogue and mutual respect, we aim to strengthen partnerships with community practitioners, ensuring that safeguarding efforts remain community-led, respecting traditions, and sustainable for future generations.

ISCR extended appreciation to Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture; Albert Vaughan, NICH President; and the Ministry of Indigenous Affairs for their continued commitment and encouragement in safeguarding and promoting the enduring traditions of our Belizean people.

World.title: New cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers begins service in Belize
World.content:
New cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers begins service in Belize

By Zoila Palma: A new cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers has officially begun their service in Belize following an oath ceremony led by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Rhonda Slusher.

The ceremony was attended by Dr. Nadine Rogers, members of the Peace Corps community and government representatives, formally welcoming the volunteers into the Peace Corps’ more than six-decade partnership with Belize.

The volunteers will serve in the Youth Development and Primary Education sectors, supporting locally led initiatives aimed at strengthening youth development and education.

Their assignments will include work with the Youth Empowered by Sports (YES) project, as well as literacy programs and other classroom-based initiatives, while living and working alongside Belizean communities.

As the Peace Corps marks 65 years of global service, the new volunteers will continue a longstanding legacy of partnership, cultural exchange and community-driven development.

World.title: Protected Areas Conservation trust convenes conservation forum
World.content:
Protected Areas Conservation trust convenes conservation forum

By Zoila Palma: The Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT) recently convened conservation partners for its “Connect. Reflect. Advance.” forum—a collaborative event designed to strengthen partnerships, celebrate achievements, and chart the future of conservation investment under the Conservation Investment Strategy 2.0.

Hosted in Belize City on July 23 and in Dangriga Town on July 24, the two days of sessions brought together protected area co-managers to exchange experiences, address shared challenges, and maximize the impact of conservation initiatives across Belize.

The “Connect. Reflect. Advance.” forum represented PACT’s commitment to fostering collaboration, transparency, and continuous learning among its partners. By creating space for open dialogue and collective problem-solving, the forum enhanced the effectiveness of ongoing investments while reinforcing a shared commitment to protecting Belize’s rich natural heritage.

PACT says that as it continues rolling out its Conservation Investment Strategy 2.0, the insights and commitments generated during these sessions will help shape future funding streams and strengthen partnerships that deliver meaningful environmental, social, and economic benefits for Belize.

World.title: International News: Fauci invokes 5th amendment during heated Senate Hearing on COVID-19 response
World.content:
International News: Fauci invokes 5th amendment during heated Senate Hearing on COVID-19 response

By Zoila Palma: Today, Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer questions from senators during a Republican-led Senate committee hearing examining his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Fauci was subpoenaed by Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has spent years accusing the retired infectious disease expert of misleading Congress and the public—allegations Fauci has rejected, ABC reports.

During the hearing, Fauci repeatedly responded to questions by saying, “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment.” The constitutional protection allows witnesses to decline to provide testimony that could potentially incriminate them and does not, by itself, amount to an admission of guilt.

Paul pressed Fauci on issues including federal funding for research in China, virus mutations and the origins of COVID-19, arguing that Fauci had helped fund dangerous research and later misled the public. Fauci, however, said he believed the hearing was intended to elicit statements that could support Paul’s repeated calls for his prosecution.

The hearing also highlighted the deep partisan divide over the pandemic and its origins.

The confrontation came as Fauci’s decision to remain silent limited direct exchanges with Paul but gave the senator greater opportunity to present his accusations without detailed responses from the witness.

World.title: Support for students
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith (right) confabs with Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange at the post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, where Johnson Smith updated the nation on the situation with Jamaican medical students in Cuba.Garfield Robinson

THE Government of Jamaica has pledged continued support for the roughly 270 Jamaican students still studying in crisis-hit Cuba, with Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith reaffirming the Government’s commitment to the students’

welfare.

Johnson Smith told a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday that her ministry has been closely monitoring the students who remain in Cuba, 40 of whom are sponsored by Cuban scholarships, which are supported by the Government of Jamaica, further noting that one private student has formally advised of his return home.

Meanwhile, she noted that more than 65 students, including five on government scholarships, have completed their medical studies for the 2025-2026 academic year.

“Three others have indicated that they are in the process of continuing their studies elsewhere through academic transfer, and we have to caveat these numbers because we understand anecdotally that others have returned, but they have not formally notified us,” Johnson Smith said.

“And this is understandable, they are there privately, and on their own steam, but just to say that we have the information…and we also have a line of communication that allows for them to not only indicate their return, but to request assistance if they so need,” said the minister.

Johnson Smith noted that those students who remain are offered pathways to repatriation should they express a desire to return.

“This is because our concern remains for their safety, well-being, and academic continuity. We know that prolonged power cuts and reduced public transportation causes challenges for their way of life, and the Government has communicated our preparedness to assist with one-way return tickets should they wish to return but have a difficulty with affordability,” she said.

“We continue to engage the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Health, as well as medical tertiary institutions on what, if anything, can be done for those who may wish to return and continue their studies here,” she added.

Many of the Cuban medical students have seen classes suspended or moved online with limited connectivity, as Cuba faces an ongoing energy crisis, worsened by a United States blockade on fuel shipments.

The island’s fuel shortages have been triggering frequent, lengthy, and unpredictable electricity interruptions, affecting not only education but also access to food, medical supplies, and transportation.

Back in February, Johnson Smith said some students had been reaching out and advised that their institutions either closed for a period, in one case for four weeks; and others said that classes had been suspended in favour of virtual studies, which saw challenges with Internet and electricity.

To maintain direct contact, Johnson Smith noted the ministry created a WhatsApp group, at that time linking roughly 320 students with officials in Kingston and the Jamaican Embassy in Havana, a move that allowed the Government to register many privately funded students who were previously outside formal channels.

In the meantime, Johnson Smith said Wednesday that the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to Cuba by contributing US$100,000 through the Caribbean Community (Caricom) as a humanitarian relief effort.

She said Jamaica joined Caricom heads of Government in continuing to express deep concern over the worsening humanitarian situation in Cuba and reaffirmed its commitment to a coordinated regional response to provide humanitarian assistance to the Cuban people.

“While speaking as long-standing friends of both the United States and Cuba, Caricom underscored in our joint single statement that civilian needs must remain the highest priority. We welcomed recent rounds of discussions between the governments and continue to advocate for constructive dialogue as the most effective path to relieve hardship on the people of Cuba,” said Johnson Smith.

The minister added that many Cuban medical professionals who had left the island following an abrupt end to the long-standing health technical cooperation arrangement in March 2026 have since returned to Jamaica and are continuing work under new arrangements with the health and wellness ministry. Johnson Smith added that those who chose to remain are still being accommodated as they continue to work under individual contracts.

“We all continue to value the significant contribution that Cuban medical professionals have made to our health sector over many years, and following the conclusion of the technical cooperation programme, you’d recall that a number of Cuban medical professionals chose to remain in Jamaica and continue to work under personal contracts,” she said.

World.title: The final innings
World.content:
People observe a minute’s silence for West Indian cricket legend Sir Garfield Sobers ahead of the third one-day international cricket match between England and India at Lord’s Cricket Ground in London on July 19, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

BRIDGETOWN, Barbados (CMC) — Garfield St Auburn Sobers played his final innings at the Kensington Oval here on Wednesday under bright sunshine for nearly three hours, still able to mesmerise local, regional and international spectators, most of whom, including Britain’s King Phillip, acknowledging that there have been few, “whose name alone brings a smile to people’s faces across Barbados, the Caribbean and the entire Commonwealth”.

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, in her “grateful from the nation” tribute at the State Service of Thanksgiving, said the visit to the Kensington Oval, “this most iconic of cricket grounds where Sir Garry’s casket was draped with the national flag of Barbados”, was to pay tribute, “but also to send a message to the future”.

She said the 89-year-old Sir Garry did not come to be the best or the first or the last, but “came to do his best and to be his best, not for the world, but for goals that he set himself, conscious that if he did that, along with whatever else everyone else did, that glory could come, victory could be assured”.

Sobers was buried one day after he would have celebrated his 90th birthday, and Mottley said that the gods would have conspired to ensure that the West Indies cricket team had defeated the visiting Pakistan test team by 90 runs on Tuesday in Trinidad and Tobago, thereby allowing the seven members of the regional team to attend the ceremony.

“I say today as we say farewell to you, Sir Garry, this is your final walk from Kensington Oval. This will be our country’s last opportunity to give you that which you became so accustomed to, a standing ovation,” Mottley said in blazing sunlight over the picturesque ground on the outskirts of the capital, Bridgetown.

“I ask each and every one of us in this Oval today …to let us stand and give Sir Garry, our Sir Garry, our hero, our beloved man. A man who guided me in my own personal journey with the confidence that I think that each and every one of us as children need to take on this world.

“We thank you for teaching us that greatness could wear humility, that excellence could still belong to ordinary people, that the dreams of a little boy from the Bayland could become the inheritance of an entire nation,” Mottley said of the man, who until July 17, was one of two Barbados living national heroes, the other being the internationally acclaimed singer, Robyn Rihanna Fenty, who was also present at the funeral.

Former West Indies captain, Brian Lara, who in April 1994 broke Sir Garry’s long-standing world record of 365 runs which he made against Pakistan in 1958, in an emotional address, described the gifted batsman as “my mentor, my dad, and my friend”.

Lara added: “First time I met you, you were Sir Sobers. Over the last few days I struggled with what I would say today, but now I am here, I realise something, this is not a sad moment, this is a moment for us to celebrate and I hope you feel the same.”

Lara said he hopes that 10 years from now when there will be a celebration of Sobers’s 100th birthday “we might also be celebrating the rebirth of West Indies cricket”.

Another former West Indies captain Sir Clive Lloyd, who at one time played alongside Sobers, said, “Today I believe we can honour Sir Garfied in ways that extend beyond statues and ceremonies, worthy those are.

“His extraordinary achievement as a fast bowler, as a left-arm spinner, in three distinct styles, as perhaps the greatest close catcher of the game ever seen, and as an incomparable batsman, should become the foundation of institutions dedicated to nurturing future generations.

“Today, we should study not only what Sir Garfield accomplished, but how he accomplished it. What inner drive compelled him to reach such heights? What vision inspired him each time he walked to the crease or began his run to the wicket? What dreams guided him as captain of the West Indies team?”

The Guyanese-born Lloyd said that these are questions worth asking because the answers can inspire generations yet unborn.

Sobers represented West Indies between 1954 and 1974 and played 93 Test matches, scoring 8,032 runs at a spectacular average of 57.78. Sobers also claimed 235 wickets at an average of 34.03 and an economy rate of 2.22. By an act of Parliament in 1998, Sobers was named as one of the 11 National Heroes of Barbados.

Two of Sobers’s children, Mathew and Daniel, recalled the influence their father had on their lives.

“Whether it was cricket, table tennis, golf, or just shooting hoops with the kids, he was blessed with rare talents few people had. But as I grew older, I realised his greatest gifts had very little to do with sport, but everything to do with the way he lived,” Mathew Sobers said.

“The world knew him as the Right, Excellent Sir Garfield St Aurbun Sobers. Many believed he was the greatest cricketer who ever lived,” he said noting, “but remarkable as those achievements were, they tell only part of the story.

“Dad was born into a Barbados still emerging from the long shadow of plantocracy and colonial rule. At a time when opportunity was limited for so many, he became living proof that excellence could come from these shores.

For his part, Daniel Sobers, who together with Matthew flew into Barbados from the United States, and with his younger sister Genevieve cutting short a visit to Australia with her mum, described his father as “the greatest”.

He said while he welcomes the avalanche of thoughts, prayers, and kind words about his father, he would like to thank all those who had been taking care of his father “during the more than 18 months of his steady decline”.

“Growing up, I never really understood the gravity of the mastery of my dad’s achievements. I was born into his life and just took them for granted. For me, it was a thing of normalcy.

“Doesn’t every dad at the age of 21 score 365 not out and hit six sixes in an over whenever he feels like it? What I also remember is that he was always busy and travelled a lot, and that I missed him when he was gone,” Daniel Sobers added.

Following the funeral, Sir Garfield Sobers, considered to have been the greatest all-rounder in cricket’s history, was given a 19-gun salute as his body was buried at the Coral Ridge Memorial Gardens on The Ridge, Christ Church Parish.

World.title: Dream Wknd, partners ready to welcome thousands to MoBay
World.content:
Mobay Mayor Richard Vernon addresses the recent launch of Dream Wknd 2026 held at Pier 1.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Dream Entertainment Limited, St James Municipal Corporation, and Jamaica Constabulary Force say all systems are in place for Dream Wknd’s inaugural staging in Montego Bay.

With months of planning and cross-agency collaboration will culminate in what is expected to be one of Jamaica’s largest entertainment events of the summer.

More than 30,000 patrons are expected to descend on the tourism capital over the coming days for the festival’s first staging outside its long-time home of Negril, bringing a significant boost to the local economy while showcasing Montego Bay’s growing capacity to host major international events.

Chairman of Dream Entertainment Kamal Bankay said organisers have spent months working alongside government agencies, venue operators, and service providers to ensure every aspect of the festival is ready ahead of Thursday’s opening.

“We have been working very closely with the venues and the planning authorities in St James,” Bankay said. “That includes the municipal corporation, the Jamaica Constabulary Force, the Ministry of Health, the Jamaica Fire Brigade, and the other agencies responsible for issuing the relevant approvals.”

He said the work has extended beyond regulatory requirements to include detailed coordination with venue operators and event partners responsible for delivering the festival experience.

“Based on where we are now, all of those preparations have been completed and the necessary systems are in place, so we’re ready to welcome patrons when the events begin on Thursday,” he said.

Bankay added that while Dream Wknd will deliver its signature entertainment experience, the festival also provides visitors with an opportunity to experience Montego Bay beyond the event venues.

“When you come to Montego Bay, just know that it’s a great city in its own right, and Dream Wknd is really there to elevate what’s already on offer,” he said. “Visitors can enjoy the city’s hotels, restaurants, beaches, and attractions throughout the weekend.”

Mayor Richard Vernon described Dream Wknd’s arrival in Montego Bay as a significant milestone for the city, saying it reinforces its standing as one of the Caribbean’s leading tourism and entertainment destinations.

“Dream Wknd’s expansion to Montego Bay is a landmark moment for Jamaica’s tourism capital,” Vernon said. “It affirms our city’s reputation as a premier entertainment destination in the Caribbean and demonstrates confidence in our ability to continue hosting world-class events, even during our most challenging times.”

Vernon said his team has worked closely with partners to ensure the city is prepared to welcome the influx of visitors. Traffic management plans have been finalised, public health protocols activated, and emergency contingencies established to support the festival weekend.

“Our hospitality sector has mobilised to meet demand, while local businesses are prepared… This readiness ensures that Dream Wknd will be a successful event and drive sustained economic activity across Montego Bay,” said Vernon.

Senior Superintendent Eron Samuels, commander of the St James Police Division, said the police have developed a comprehensive security plan in partnership with other stakeholders.

“Our objective is to create a safe environment where patrons can enjoy the festivities while residents and visitors continue to feel secure,” Samuels said.

He encouraged patrons to celebrate responsibly by planning their transportation in advance, avoiding drinking and driving, securing their personal belongings, remaining aware of their surroundings and following the instructions of police officers, event security personnel and emergency responders.

“Our message is simple: Enjoy the event, make lasting memories, but make safety your priority,” he said.

In addition to extensive logistical preparations, organisers say patrons can also expect an elevated festival experience through the involvement of Dream WKND’s major brand partners, each bringing unique activations designed to complement the music and entertainment.

Red Stripe and its portfolio of brands will deliver vibrant social spaces across four signature events: Guinness at Dream Live, Casamigos at Daydreams, Red Stripe at YUSH, and Smirnoff at Igloo. Meanwhile, the Campari Group will bring premium activations, signature cocktail experiences, and interactive brand engagements to Wet ‘N Wild with Magnum, Foul Play with J Wray & Nephew, and Xodus Remedy presented by Campari.

Festivalgoers can also look forward to high-energy experiences from Boom Energy Drink, whose touchpoints are designed to keep the excitement going throughout the weekend. Mother’s will round out the culinary experience with specially curated dishes prepared throughout the weekend, providing hearty, flavourful meal options to keep patrons fuelled while they enjoy the overall festival atmosphere.

Dream Entertainment says the collective investment by its corporate partners reflects a shared commitment to delivering a world-class entertainment experience, with immersive brand experiences carefully integrated into the festival to ensure patrons enjoy much more than just the performances onstage.

World.title: Safety or red tape?
World.content:
DALRYMPLE-PHILIBERT... said any organisation introducing a programme for children has a duty to satisfy itself that those involved are suitable.

A spirited debate erupted during a sitting of Parliament’s joint select committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act on Wednesday, after Government Senator Sherene Golding-Campbell questioned why licensed psychologists, who are already vetted by their professional regulatory body, must undergo additional background checks before being allowed to work with children in the Child Diversion Programme.

However, committee members, including chairman Delroy Chuck, argued that the additional scrutiny is essential because vulnerable children are involved, insisting that no safeguard should be overlooked when selecting professionals to work in the programme.

The disagreement emerged as the committee examined provisions of the Act dealing with how counsellors and psychologists are approved to provide services under the Child Diversion Programme, which seeks to rehabilitate children who come into conflict with the law rather than exposing them to the formal court system.

Under the existing law, the minister is empowered to approve counsellors and psychologists for use in the programme. The legislation also requires standards and procedures to be set for the operation of diversion services.

Golding-Campbell questioned whether that approval process was necessary for psychologists who are already licensed to practise under Jamaican law.

“If they’re registered under the Act, what is the purpose of a background check on a psychologist? I’m not understanding that,” she asked.

Director of the Child Diversion Branch in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Venisa Clarke explained that the programme uses a range of mental health professionals, including psychologists, counsellors, clinical social workers, and guidance counsellors.

She said the background checks are carried out not because the professionals are unqualified, but because they will be working closely with vulnerable children.

“Every psychologist that touches base with the Child Diversion Office or contacts us, we have a list of things that are required. We have a checklist that they have to meet certain criteria. Once that is done, we indicate to them that we are now going to move to get the approval to engage. The first aspect of that approval is that a background check has to be done as well, and we have to see that they are certified,” Clarke explained.

She said the background check includes more than a criminal record search.

“For the mental health service providers, we engage a private member of society that does that for us. It includes a visit to their community, getting information from NIB [National Intelligence Bureau], as well as a sex offender registry, a whole list of things, and the report includes if they find any adverse traces or anything of that sort,” she added.

Golding-Campbell, however, argued that the process appeared to duplicate checks already carried out by the bodies responsible for licensing professionals. She also questioned whether the programme was making the best use of limited public resources.

“I appreciate that it’s children, but if these professionals are registered, they’re registered. If they have a valid registration under the Act, they’re registered. I’m not understanding why we would commit resources to a private investigator to find out whether or not they have convictions,” she queried further.

The senator also questioned why the minister should have the power to approve individual psychologists and counsellors if they have already met the legal requirements to practice in Jamaica.

Her concerns were met with resistance from several committee members.

Chuck acknowledged that professionally registered psychologists may require less scrutiny than other groups, but said the ministry still has a responsibility to ensure every person working with children can be trusted.

“You don’t know which of these personnel could abuse the child. And therefore, the background check is absolutely important… The last thing we would want is we put the child to interact with a mentor, and the mentor turns out to be a paedophile,” he said.

Member of Parliament for Portland Eastern Isat Buchanan also defended the practice, arguing that professional registration alone cannot guarantee that a person poses no risk to children.

“Background checks for the purpose of child diversion are about adverse findings. There are persons who have come in conflict with the law that have not been brought before the court because other things would have happened…So if we are protecting the child, Minister, respectfully, you sit in the chair right now. It is the approval by you, because if anything should happen I will be the first to say, ‘How could the minister make this happen? Heads should roll!’, and I will be the first to say ‘Resign, resign, resign’,” he expressed.

State minister in the Ministry of Justice Marisa Dalrymple-Philibert similarly backed the existing approach, saying any organisation introducing a programme for children has a duty to satisfy itself that those involved are suitable.

However, Golding-Campbell maintained that her concern was not with protecting children but with making sure the system is logical and consistent. She argued that if the programme believes extra vetting is necessary, then it should not happen only once at the beginning.

“If it is that you want to be satisfied that they are safe people for children separate and apart from their registration under law governed by another body, then it must be something that you’re telling me you’re satisfying yourself of periodically, because to satisfy yourself when they are approved does not hold for the entire time that they participate in the programme. Being good in 2022 doesn’t mean that I haven’t committed some offence that would disturb you in 2025,” she said.

That argument appeared to win some support from Chuck, who agreed that repeat checks should be considered.

Clarke also welcomed the suggestion, confirming that, while background checks are currently mandatory before a professional joins the programme, the ministry would consider introducing periodic reviews.

World.title: LEAPING TO HISTORY
World.content:
Tajay Gayle (Photo: AFP)

TAJAY Gayle created history on Wednesday when he won Jamaica’s first-ever men’s long jump gold medal at the Commonwealth Games (CWG).

Shot putter Lloydricia Cameron claimed a bronze medal at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, as Jamaica’s medal tally went up to four — inclusive of three gold and a bronze — at the 23rd edition of the Games.

Romaine Beckford and Demario Prince had opened Jamaica’s medal account on Monday with gold medals in the men’s high jump and 110m hurdles, respectively.

Expectations are high for more medals on Thursday with finals in the women’s triple jump and discus throw competitions.

After placing fourth at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia, Gayle jumped 8.15m (1.5m/s) to become the first Jamaican man to win a long jump competition. He is the first Jamaican man to win a medal at the Games since Wesley Clayton won back-to-back bronze in 1962 and 1966.

India’s Sreeshankar took consecutive silver medals after a best mark of 8.09m (1.3m/s), just ahead of Stephen Mackenzie of Scotland who was third with 8.08m (0.9m/s). Jamaican Jordan Turner was ninth with 7.65m (0.1m/s).

Cameron, who won her first national championships title this year, improved on her fourth-place finish from four years ago in Birmingham, England, taking the bronze with a best of 17.87m in the final round to eclipse Manpreet Kaur of India.

Canada’s two-time World Athletics Indoor champion Sarah Mitton defended her title with an effort of 19.88m. Nigeria’s 19-year-old Jessica Oji took the silver medal with 17.87m, getting the edge over Cameron with a better second throw.

National champion Ackelia Smith and NCAA winner Shantae Foreman are set to take on world leader and Olympic champion Thea Lafond of Dominica in the women’s triple jump on Thursday.

Jamaica’s Samantha Hall is the Commonwealth leader in the women’s discus throw and will start as pre-championships favourite going into the final.

There will also be qualifying in the 100m hurdles in which Kerrica Hill and Megan Simmonds are set to compete. In the men’s triple jump Jordan Scott, who is ranked number one, is also down to feature.

Kelly Ann Beckford qualified for the final of the women’s 800m after placing third in her semi-finals in 1:59.96, beaten to the finish line by Lilian Odira (1:59.39) of Kenya and Shafiqua Maloney (1:59.81) of St Vincent and the Grenadines.

Adelle Tracey was fourth in her heat in 2:01.54 for 10th overall.

Other Jamaicans, including 200m and women’s 400m hurdles runners, progressed past the first round of their respective events on Wednesday.

National champion Sanique Walker and Shiann Salmon, the latter who was second four years ago in Birmingham, topped the qualifying in the women’s 400m hurdles.

Walker won her heat in 54.83 seconds and Salmon topped hers in 55.30 to booked places in Friday’s final.

National champion Assinie Wilson was second in his first round heat in the men’s 400m hurdles in 49.19.

Lavanya Williams and Alana Reid were also the fastest in the women’s 200m first round.

Williams ran 22.91 (0.8m/s) to win heat five and national champion Reid clocked 22.95 (1.7m/s) to claim heat six as they made safe passage through to Thursday’s semi-finals.

All three Jamaican men also advanced in the 200m.

Christopher Taylor was second in his heat in 20.36 (1.6m/s), the same time given to Ghana’s Joseph Paul Amoah, who was declared the winner.

Roshawn Clarke won his heat in 20.56 (1/0m/s) and Jevaughn Powell recorded a wind-aided 20.28 (2.6m/s) to top his heat.

World.title: Chef Colin Brown’s HOMECOMING CHAÎNE FEAST
World.content:
Yellowfin tuna crudo with lime-ginger marinade, Scotch bonnet oil, ripe mango salsa and breadfruit crisp (Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

Sun-kissed afternoon, the hum of conversation, and the clink of glasses set the scene at Uncorked Ochi at Drax Hall on Sunday, July 26 as Chaîne des Rôtisseurs Jamaïque, Select Brands, and Uncorked hosted a celebratory bistro brunch showcasing the return of Chef Colin Brown to Jamaican shores. Brown — back from an international run of kitchens — teamed with Uncorked’s culinary team to present a lively fusion of island flavours and classic French techniques that won praise from members and guests alike.

The cold and seafood station opened the meal with refined island flair: Yellowfin tuna crudo brightened with a lime-ginger marinade, Scotch bonnet oil, ripe mango salsa, and a crisp of breadfruit; and an escoveitch conch paired with calabash lobster, spiced pickled vegetables, allspice, and lime zest that married Caribbean acidities with steely seafood sweetness.

The opening of the smoked and slow-roast station followed. A pimento-smoked salmon with a rustic salsa; golden goat, glazed with Appleton rum and finished with a nutmeg-thyme jus offered deep, caramelised rum notes; and Blue Mountain coffee-crusted pork belly, lacquered in a tamarind-molasses glaze balanced bitter, sweet and savoury. Braised oxtail croquettes, stuffed with a butter-bean purée with chive oil, provided a textural and flavourful nod to Jamaica’s comfort-cook traditions, while a live action station with pimento-smoked roasted leg of lamb, scented with rosemary, orange zest and tarragon, rounded out the roast offerings.

Side dishes and local provisions were treated with equal care: roasted sweet potatoes and breadfruit crowned with coconut butter and toasted pimento, herbed yam croquettes, creamy coconut rice with gungo peas, callaloo-pak choi sautéed with ginger, garlic and island five-spice, and an inventive green banana risotto studded with aged local artisan cheese. These accompaniments anchored the menu in terroir while supporting the international techniques on display.

Dessert showcased Jamaica’s signature ingredients in elegant formats: Wray & Nephew rum and gingerbread pudding bathed in warm coconut custard, a sorrel-hibiscus panna cotta with candied ginger, and a guava tart in flaky coconut pastry. Sweet finishes were complemented by a chilled limoncello cooler pairing that cut through the richness.

Select Brands curated the beverage pours, pairing the menu with a sparkling and wine line-up that included Veuve Clicquot Brut NV, Kettmeir Pinot Grigio 2024, Terra Alpina Chardonnay 2022, Aqua di Venus Rosé, Tassajara Pinot Noir 2022 and Dominio Fournier 2020. The thoughtful beverage selection underscored the brunch’s balance of celebration and culinary craft.

The event was both a welcome-home for Chef Brown and a statement of culinary collaboration — a tasteful fusion that celebrated Jamaica’s pantry while leaning into French technique and presentation, a thrust Brown is quick to emphasise in the Jamaican culinary space.

“We have to cook our own food, add our cultural perspective and use the techniques from France, Italy and we’ll become masters by taking an indigenous cuisine and refining it. For today’s menu we used the Seville orange, rice vinegar, Mirin, sushi ginger, ripe mango, tomato and we boiled the breadfruit in the skin, sliced thinly, fried it to make a nice crisp and this came out really well for the yellow fin tuna. escoveitch conch and lobster, we made a lobster bisque for the base, boil it and season only with Scotch bonnet powder, sear it, keeping it fresh and nice. For the conch we cooked it for hours and sliced it thinly, tossed and fried keeping it crispy,” Brown explained.

“The salmon was done of more a jerk style but with more kick to it. Everyone is more use to curry goat, but we slow-cooked the goat with Appleton rum, nutmeg and thyme, making it a well-balanced dish. The crispy pork belly was cooked in Blue Mountain coffee jerk for two and half hours and glazed with June plum and lime and dusted with Blue Mountain coffee, giving you the sweet, sour, coffee flavour and the jerk. The oxtail was also slow cooked and the lamb leg we marinated for three days,” Brown added.

World.title: Jamaica snatch last minute draw against Panama in U20
World.content:
Jaquan Brown of Jamaica celebrates his equaliser in the young Reggae Boyz' Concacaf Under-20 Championship match against Panama on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. The game ended 2-2. (Photo: Concacaf/Instagram)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica rallied from two goals down to earn a courageous draw against Panama in their Concacaf U20 Championships Group C at Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico on Wednesday.

The result kept Jamaica’s hopes of advancing to the quarterfinals alive as they are on four points, one more than Canada who will play Honduras in the second game, while Panama are on one point from two games.

Jamaica are also third in the overall rankings that include teams from the other groups, only behind the USA and Mexico, both of who have won their first two games.

Desperate to earn a win after losing 3-0 to Canada on Sunday, Panama got off to a fast start and were ahead 2-0 after 22 minutes with goals from Moisés Richards in the 13th minute and Carlos Rodriguez in the 22nd minute.

It could have been worse had VAR not ruled out another goal for Panama in the 36th minute.

Jahmarie Nolan, who had scored the first goal in the 2-1 win over Honduras, pulled a goal back for Jamaica in the 62nd minute before Jaquan Brown headed home a freekick from second half substitute Jamione Lyle in time added.

It was the second time in a row that Jamaica scored on the final play of the game, in time added, after Brandon Bent had scored the winner against Honduras in time added.

The coaches had made one change to the starting team, Che Gardner of Stockport County replacing Sean Leighton.

Starting team:

Joshua Grant, Jaquan Brown, Jahmarie Nolan, Jermaine Young, Jabarie

Howell, Jahmani Bell, Che Gardner, Duwayne Burgher, Santana

World.title: US-Iran war looms over Britain’s economy
World.content:
“Inflation has fallen faster than we’ve expected, but the conflict in the Middle East continues to mean high and volatility energy prices,” said BoE Governor Andrew Bailey.

In the U.K. and EU, the U.S.-Iran temporary ceasefire brought hopes to policymakers that the impact of the conflict could be short-lived, with signs of resilience in the economy, amid lower services and food inflation, slowing wage growth and a soft labor market.

The European Central Bank was the first major central bank to raise rates in June in a bid to ensure price stability, but held in its July meeting after eurozone inflation came in lower than expected last month. The U.K., too, saw inflation falling in June — to 2.6 percent — before the conflict re-escalated.

But, with Britain predicted to take the biggest economic hit of any major country from the Iran war, the path ahead appears particularly uncertain, according to the central bank's projections, and will depend just how far energy prices spiral driven by the on-again off-again nature of the war.

"The U.K. is an open economy, so obviously we look at world conditions and of course in some ways never more so than at the moment, given what's going on in the wider world and particularly the conflict in the Gulf," Bailey told journalists in a press conference following the MPC decision.

The central bank modeled various scenarios to assess the possible impact of the ongoing war. In an adverse scenario, where there is a repeated re-escalation of the conflict, prices start sticking throughout the economy and inflation peaks at 4.5 percent in the second quarter of 2027.

World.title: Spain, France, UK warn megafires show climate change is ‘threatening our way of life’
World.content:
Members of the Emergency Military Unit use controlled burns to halt the spread of wildfires in the Madrid border region on July 28, 2026. | Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty Images

In joint statements, the three countries reaffirmed their commitment to fighting global warming.

BRUSSELS — The massive blazes raging in Spain and France epitomize the threat climate change is posing to Europe, the British government said in joint statements issued with the two fire-stricken countries overnight.

Wildfires have burned tens of thousands of hectares near Madrid and Bordeaux this week, razing hundreds of homes and displacing more than 300,000 people in one of the biggest fire-related evacuations Europe has seen to date.

Blazes have also erupted in other parts of the continent, which is suffering from widespread drought after Europe’s hottest June on record, including in the United Kingdom.

World.title: EU launches €30B push to build 7 massive AI data centers
World.content:
The Commission will select the winning bids by early next year, after which companies will have 18 months to build them. Those angling for a smaller project could receive up to €1 billion in public funding, while the larger projects could receive up to €2 billion.

The EU has put in place “the largest public-private partnership” to ensure funding, a senior Commission official told reporters Thursday. The Commission has earmarked €1 billion so far and foresees a further €4 billion under the next long-term EU budget — although it admitted the latter amount remains uncertain given ongoing budget talks.

Public funding should not exceed 35 percent of the total investment — the Commission says that combined with private funds, the investment could amount to €30 billion.

EU legislators and industry observers have raised questions about the plans, including whether there will be sufficient demand from AI companies for the compute power generated by the data centers, and whether they will perpetuate dependency on foreign tech given that advanced computing chips are all U.S.-made.

The senior Commission official rebutted that criticism, saying the current infrastructure is already “saturated in demand.”

The official acknowledged that U.S. AI chip providers such as Nvidia are “omnipresent,” but said other providers could help with the next phase of upgrading the facilities.

World.title: Tusk: ‘Everything indicates’ Russian cruise missile hit Poland
World.content:
The object was detected moving westward through Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m., according to the country's Operational Command. An F-16 fighter jet was sent to identify and intercept it, but the object disappeared from radar six minutes later, before it could be identified.

A Mi-24 attack helicopter subsequently located the probable crash site in an undeveloped area near Tarnawa-Kolonia in the Lublin province — a region near the Ukrainian border. Police found a crater and debris in a field about 2 kilometers from the nearest buildings after residents reported a loud explosion, according to local police. No casualties were reported.

"This is yet another clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine’s air defense now is urgent and serves as a guarantee for the protection of the entire Euro-Atlantic community," Sybiha said on X.

EU Council President António Costa described "Russia’s aggression" as "a threat to the security of Europe as a whole."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed eight people were killed during the strikes on social media, adding that three children and their parents in the Dnipro region were among the victims.

He also reiterated his call for help from Ukraine’s allies. “Untimely assistance and delays in the delivery of anti-ballistic missiles lead to this kind of destruction, these kinds of casualties that, unfortunately, we are seeing today,” he wrote.

Ferdinand Knapp and Victor Jack contributed to this report.

This story has been updated.

World.title: Burnham’s blitz: Sam and Anne’s verdict
World.content:
Andy Burnham has thrown the future of legalising assisted dying into doubt. After telling Sam Coates that he does not want legislation to proceed until social care and palliative care are “fixed”.



Supporters of the bill insist they are pressing ahead. But has the Prime Minister’s intervention made its passage through Parliament far less likely?

Sam and Anne examine what Burnham’s comments mean for MPs ahead of the crucial September vote.

And, before Sam and Anne take some time off over summer, what do they make of Burnham’s first two weeks?
