Las cartas de los lectores tratan sobre la progresiva desaparición de los quioscos de prensa en los pueblos, la falta de políticas de prevención de los incendios forestales, el negacionismo climático y la masificación turística en Mallorca

Opinión de un lector sobre una información publicada por el diario o un hecho noticioso. Dirigidas al director del diario y seleccionadas y editadas por el equipo de opinión

Tres librerías del centro, todas cerradas. Domingo de junio. Montilla (Córdoba), unas 22.000 almas. Parece misión imposible comprar prensa escrita. Periferia de la capital del Turia, Sedaví, 11.000 personas y cuesta adquirir periódicos. Ni en los bares. Los pides mientras consumes y te miran raro. Julio, Siete Aguas (Valencia). Algo más de 1.000 habitantes, multiplicados por diez en verano. Ningún punto de venta de periódicos. Cerró el quiosco hace años. Los últimos ejemplares se vendían en una carnicería. No se encuentran, también hace tiempo, ni a dos kilómetros, en una gasolinera de la autovía. Allí me informan que en otra estación de servicio, en Requena (21.000 habitantes), sí que tienen. Son los únicos de esa población. Tendría que hacer 30 kilómetros. Por casualidad, en otra localidad, Cheste, 9.000 habitantes, descubro una papelería-quiosco. Compro, por fin, un periódico. Felicito a la propietaria. Me cuenta que al lado, en Chiva, 19.000 censados, nadie vende ejemplares. Un consuelo, volver a casa, Centelles (Barcelona), 8.000 vecinos, sabiendo que en la librería-papelería Magazine aún podré disfrutar de un lujo: comprar cualquier cabecera, intentar comprender el mundo leyendo en papel.

Antonio Salido Contreras. Centelles (Barcelona)

Cansados y desprotegidos

Las personas que vivimos en el medio rural estamos cansadas de que nos den lecciones desde el sillón de la capital, mientras hacen scroll y escriben comentarios en las redes. El medio rural está desprotegido, olvidado, desatendido. Se abandonan los pueblos porque es insostenible vivir en un territorio con falta de oportunidades, donde los recursos son cada vez más precarios. El fuego no entiende de territorios, siempre va por delante. Hoy se quema Madrid, pero en Castilla y León llevamos años contemplando cómo el fuego arrasa nuestra tierra, llevándose cultivos, bosques, ganado, fauna salvaje, hasta viviendas. Negar el cambio climático es una temeridad que no podemos permitirnos. La prevención debería ser una prioridad máxima. Las personas del medio rural estamos cansadas de ver cómo arde nuestro territorio por pura desidia.

Ana Belén Pérez Villa. Soria

Negacionismo climático

Me indigna que algunos políticos carguen con el mantra de “el clima siempre ha cambiado” para justificar lo que está sucediendo con los incendios forestales que arrasan parte del territorio. Como geólogo sé que el clima ha cambiado a lo largo del tiempo, pero estos cambios siempre han sucedido a lo largo de miles, cientos de miles e incluso millones de años. Es decir, unos periodos lo suficientemente largos para que la naturaleza evolucione y se adapte.

Óscar Ercilla Herrero. Madrid

Mallorca en venta

Mientras veía, el pasado domingo, la manifestación contra la masificación del turismo en Mallorca, me dio por pensar que los médicos, profesores, camareros y otros profesionales, al no poder alquilar un piso cerca de su trabajo, deberían optar por trabajar en la península, pues al fin se conseguirá lo que parece que se pretende: que en Mallorca solo vivan turistas.

Vicente Quijano Álvarez. Madrid

World.title: Benidorm, Alicante o la Costa Dorada: cinco escapadas al Mediterráneo más secreto
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

A pocos kilómetros de las playas más concurridas se esconden montañas, fortalezas medievales, arrozales y pueblos donde el verano transcurre a otro ritmo

Hay una imagen del Mediterráneo que todos conocemos. Es la de las playas que se llenan al amanecer, los paseos marítimos repletos de gente paseando, las terrazas abiertas frente al horizonte azul y ese rumor constante de las olas que acompaña las vacaciones desde hace generaciones. Pero existe otro Mediterráneo, el que comienza precisamente cuando el mar desaparece del retrovisor.

Desde cualquier playa levantina, para quienes tengan un poco de curiosidad viajera, también hay alternativas. Basta conducir media hora tierra adentro para descubrir que muchas de las grandes costas españolas esconden un segundo viaje, menos evidente y, precisamente por eso, más sorprendente. Son escapadas breves que cambian el salitre por el aroma de los pinos, las sombrillas por castillos medievales, las calas por bancales de olivos, las avenidas junto al mar por pueblos donde aún se conversa al fresco cuando cae la tarde. El litoral puede ser un destino vacacional, pero también una puerta de entrada a otros destinos mucho menos masivos del interior.

Más información Guía definitiva del Gran Cañón del Colorado: cómo organizar la visita paso a paso

Desde Benidorm se asciende a montañas que parecen suspendidas sobre el Mediterráneo; desde Alicante, una cadena de fortalezas recuerda siglos de fronteras cambiantes; desde la Costa Dorada, el agua dulce del Ebro dibuja uno de los paisajes más singulares de Europa; desde la Costa del Sol, la Alpujarra ofrece un refugio de pueblos blancos y barrancos verdes; y desde La Manga murciana, el Valle de Ricote no queda muy lejos y conserva un paisaje agrícola heredero de Al-Ándalus que parece ajeno al paso del tiempo.

Más información en www.lonelyplanet.es

1. Benidorm también mira hacia la montaña

Pocas ciudades están tan asociadas al turismo de playa como Benidorm, pero no todo es arena y tumbonas: detrás de su inconfundible perfil de rascacielos se levanta una de las comarcas montañosas más espectaculares del litoral mediterráneo. En menos de una hora la carretera abandona el bullicio urbano para serpentear entre almendros, bancales de piedra seca y paredes de roca caliza que anuncian la entrada en la Marina Baixa interior.

El primer alto suele ser Guadalest, uno de esos pueblos cuya silueta parece diseñada para aparecer en una postal. Su castillo se encarama sobre una peña inaccesible y domina un embalse de intensas tonalidades turquesa que contrasta con el paisaje seco de las sierras cercanas. Pasear por sus calles empedradas permite entender por qué este pequeño enclave fue durante siglos un lugar estratégico para controlar los pasos entre la costa y el interior.

El embalse de Guadalest en Alicante. Alamy / Cordon Press

Pero el verdadero atractivo aparece cuando se continúa el viaje hacia el valle de Guadalest, que conecta con una sucesión de pequeñas localidades como Benimantell, Confrides o Castell de Castells, donde la vida transcurre a un ritmo completamente distinto al del litoral. Aquí los senderistas encuentran algunas de las rutas más conocidas de la provincia, como las que ascienden a la Serrella o al macizo de Aitana, la montaña más alta de Alicante.

Desde muchos de sus miradores resulta difícil creer que el Mediterráneo esté a apenas unos kilómetros. En días despejados, sin embargo, la línea azul reaparece en el horizonte como un recordatorio constante de la cercanía entre dos mundos completamente distintos.

Familias en las Fuentes del Algar. Petr Svarc (Getty Images)

El viaje puede terminar en las Fuentes del Algar, donde el agua vuelve a cobrar protagonismo en forma de cascadas y pozas naturales. Después de una mañana entre montañas, sumergirse en estas aguas frescas resulta casi tan mediterráneo como hacerlo en una cala.

2. Alicante y la frontera de piedra

Si existe una ruta capaz de explicar buena parte de la historia del sureste peninsular es la de los Castillos del Vinalopó. Desde Alicante solo hay que conducir en dirección noroeste para adentrarse en un corredor natural que durante siglos fue frontera entre reinos musulmanes y cristianos. El resultado es una extraordinaria concentración de fortalezas que aún hoy dominan pueblos y montañas.

La primera gran parada suele ser Villena. Sobre la ciudad emerge el castillo de la Atalaya, una poderosa construcción almohade reforzada tras la conquista cristiana, que es la prueba de la importancia estratégica del valle y de las rutas comerciales que atravesaban este territorio.

El castillo de la Atalaya en Villena. Alamy / Cordon Press

La carretera continúa hacia Sax. Su castillo parece surgir directamente de la roca, mientras que el casco urbano se extiende a sus pies formando un conjunto armónico. Muy cerca aparece Petrer, con un castillo que nos transporta directamente al ambiente de las antiguas fortalezas fronterizas.

El castillo de Sax. Alamy / Cordon Press

Elda añade un componente industrial a la ruta gracias a su histórica tradición zapatera, mientras Novelda introduce un cambio inesperado de paisaje. Además de su modernista Santuario de Santa María Magdalena, inspirado en las formas del modernismo catalán, el municipio se encuentra rodeado por cultivos de uva embolsada, un sistema agrícola único que protege cada racimo con una bolsa de papel durante su maduración.

El recorrido permite descubrir que en la provincia de Alicante hay mucho más que playas: hay historias de caballeros, comerciantes, fortalezas islámicas, órdenes militares y antiguas fronteras que moldearon el territorio durante siglos. Y cada castillo es de cierta forma un capítulo de esta historia.

3. El Delta del Ebro: un paisaje de agua

Quien pasa unos días en la Costa Dorada de Tarragona suele pensar en largas playas de arena fina, pequeñas calas y patrimonio romano. Sin embargo, hacia el sur aparece un paisaje completamente diferente. El Delta del Ebro es una de esas geografías donde la naturaleza parece estar en permanente construcción: el río deposita sedimentos, el mar modifica la costa y las lagunas cambian con las estaciones.

El Delta es toda una invitación a un viaje lento. Las bicicletas sustituyen al coche en muchos recorridos, permitiendo avanzar entre canales, campos y observatorios desde los que contemplar flamencos, garzas, espátulas o águilas pescadoras. Las carreteras cruzan inmensos arrozales que en primavera se transforman en espejos de agua y en verano adquieren un verde intenso antes de dorarse con la llegada de la cosecha.

Flamencos en la reserva de el Delta del Ebro en Tarragona. Alamy / Cordon Press

La desembocadura del Ebro constituye uno de los grandes espectáculos del Mediterráneo español. Allí donde el río termina, comienza un delicado ecosistema donde el agua dulce y la salada conviven en un equilibrio cambiante. También la gastronomía refleja esa mezcla. El arroz aparece en múltiples versiones, acompañado de anguilas, mejillones, ostras o pescados capturados pocas horas antes. Comer frente a una laguna mientras el viento mueve suavemente los cañaverales ayuda a comprender que el Delta no es solo un espacio protegido: es una forma de vivir ligada al agua.

Al atardecer, cuando miles de aves regresan a los humedales y el cielo adquiere tonalidades rosadas, el paisaje alcanza una serenidad difícil de encontrar en otros lugares del litoral mediterráneo.

4. La Alpujarra desconocida desde la Costa del Sol

Para muchos viajeros, la Costa del Sol termina donde empiezan las montañas. En realidad, es ahí donde comienza uno de los cambios de paisaje más sorprendentes del sur peninsular. En apenas hora y media de carretera, el ambiente costero deja paso a barrancos profundos, castañares, acequias centenarias y pueblos blancos que parecen colgar de las laderas de Sierra Nevada.

Una calle en el pueblo de Cartajima. Alamy / Cordon Press

La Alpujarra suele asociarse a Granada, pero su vertiente occidental, compartida con Málaga, conserva rincones mucho menos transitados. Pequeñas localidades como Júzcar, Cartajima o Alpandeire anuncian la transición hacia un territorio donde las huellas andalusíes siguen presentes en la arquitectura popular y en los sistemas tradicionales de aprovechamiento del agua. Más adelante aparecen pueblos emblemáticos como Pampaneira, Bubión o Capileira, construidos sobre fuertes pendientes y caracterizados por sus tejados planos, chimeneas cilíndricas y calles estrechas adaptadas a la montaña.

El pueblo de Júzcar en Málaga. Alamy / Cordon Press

El gran lujo de un viaje por esta zona es dormir con las ventanas abiertas con el aire fresco de Sierra Nevada. O caminar entre terrazas agrícolas sostenidas por muros de piedra seca. Los senderos siguen antiguas acequias que todavía distribuyen el agua del deshielo mediante un ingenioso sistema heredado de época islámica.

Cada curva de la montaña nos descubre un nuevo barranco, una iglesia mudéjar, un bosque de castaños o un mirador desde el que el Mediterráneo reaparece a lo lejos como una fina línea azul.

5. El Valle de Ricote, el último jardín andalusí

La Manga del Mar Menor representa uno de los paisajes más característicos del Mediterráneo español y del veraneo de toda la vida. Sin embargo, poco más de una hora hacia el interior aparece un escenario completamente inesperado, no muy lejos de la capital murciana: el del Valle de Ricote, uno de los últimos grandes paisajes agrícolas vinculados al legado morisco. El río Segura atraviesa una sucesión de huertas donde prosperan limoneros, naranjos, granados y palmeras gracias a un sofisticado sistema de regadío que hunde sus raíces en la ingeniería hidráulica de Al-Ándalus.

Pueblos como Ricote, Ojós, Ulea, Villanueva del Río Segura, Blanca o Abarán mantienen una identidad muy marcada. Las casas blancas ascienden por las laderas, las acequias siguen alimentando los cultivos y el ritmo cotidiano parece ajeno al turismo masivo del litoral. En Abarán sobreviven además varias norias históricas, algunas todavía en funcionamiento, que recuerdan la importancia del agua en una región donde cada gota ha sido siempre un recurso precioso.

El paisaje sorprende por su contraste: en pocas horas se pasa de las playas abiertas al Mediterráneo a un territorio de huertas, palmerales y montañas áridas que enmarcan un auténtico oasis. El patrimonio gastronómico también habla de esa mezcla cultural: frutas de hueso, cítricos, verduras de temporada, aceite de oliva y dulces de tradición morisca completan una experiencia profundamente ligada al territorio.

Una de las mejores formas de recorrer el valle consiste en seguir la Vía Verde del Chicharra o navegar en piragua por algunos tramos tranquilos del Segura.

World.title: Se buscan las maravillas contemporáneas del mundo y puedes elegir: el Guggenheim Bilbao podría ser la primera de España
World.content:
El Museo Guggenheim en Bilbao, la Torre Eiffel en París o el Gran Museo Egipcio en Guiza podrían ser parte de las siete maravillas contemporáneas, si el mundo así lo decide. El Consejo Mundial de Viajes y Turismo (WTTC) está buscando la siguiente generación de maravillas del mundo y, por primera vez, todo el que quiera podrá participar en la elección de estos monumentos. Una iniciativa que busca identificar y celebrar los aeropuertos, resorts, estatuas, óperas, museos, puentes y cualquier centro turístico o edificios creados a manos de ingenieros, arquitectos y artistas, a partir del siglo XIX, que han impulsado el turismo sostenible y que redefinirán el futuro de los viajes.

La WTTC, organización que trabaja con gobiernos y empresas para apoyar el crecimiento del turismo mundial sostenible, busca reconocer la importancia arquitectónica y cultural de estos monumentos, así como su impacto en las economías locales, la atracción de inversiones, la creación de empleo y que ayudan a redefinir la identidad de naciones enteras. La máxima autoridad global en turismo lanza ahora esta campaña para reconocer tanto a iconos mundialmente famosos como a lugares emblemáticos emergentes que han tenido y tendrán el potencial de dar paso a la nueva generación de destinos turísticos.

La campaña durará un año y se dividirá en cuatro etapas. Desde el pasado 7 de julio, las nominaciones están abiertas al público y los viajeros podrán proponer a sus candidatos en la página web de la WWTC hasta el próximo 7 de enero, cuando se anunciarán los 70 nominados seleccionados y comenzará la votación pública. Después, el 7 de abril de 2027, la lista se reducirá a 30 finalistas. Y, finalmente, el 7 de julio de 2027 se revelarán las siete maravillas contemporáneas del mundo. Los criterios para nominar palacios, instituciones, rascacielos o estadios son: que estén hechos por manos humanas; que hayan sido construidos entre 1801 y la actualidad; que atraigan al mundo, con responsabilidad, y creen oportunidades donde se encuentran; y su fama no importa, pueden participar desde las obras más conocidas hasta las aún por descubrir.

El hotel Marina Bay Sands en Singapur. fiftymm99 (getty images)

“En un momento en que los gobiernos de todo el mundo buscan nuevas fuentes de crecimiento y resiliencia, el WTTC lanza esta campaña para destacar el valor de los atractivos turísticos de primer nivel como infraestructura estratégica”, se lee en la descipción en la página web. “La selección de las 7 Maravillas Contemporáneas del Mundo también pone de relieve cómo la colaboración público-privada puede crear lugares emblemáticos de primer nivel que generen crecimiento futuro y mejoren la experiencia del visitante”.

“La capacidad de asombro no es algo que la humanidad haya dejado de crear hace siglos. Cada generación deja su huella en el mundo. Por ello invitamos a personas de todo el mundo a reconocer los monumentos que han definido la era moderna y que seguirán inspirando nuevas formas de experimentar el mundo”, declara Gloria Guevara, presidenta y directora ejecutiva de WTTC en la página web. “Los atractivos turísticos más influyentes hacen mucho más que atraer visitantes. Crean empleo, estimulan la inversión, apoyan a las empresas locales, fortalecen las comunidades y realzan la proyección internacional de los destinos. Queremos mostrar cómo las inversiones visionarias en infraestructura turística y patrimonio cultural pueden generar un valor económico y social duradero para las futuras generaciones”, añade.

La Estatua de la Libertad en Nueva York, los rascacielos Marina Bay Sands o el Aeropuerto Internacional de Singapur, el Palacio de Bellas Artes o el Museo Soumaya en Ciudad de México, la Esfera en Las Vegas o la Ópera de Sídney son algunas de las propuestas del Consejo. Y en España, usuarios en las redes sociales proponen el Museo del Prado o el Estadio Santiago Bernabéu en Madrid, las Setas o la Plaza de España en Sevilla, o el Museo de las Ciencias Príncipe Felipe en Valencia. Aunque la favorita parece ser la Sagrada Familia en Barcelona.

World.title: University launches ethics probe into Red Bull professor’s work
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Utrecht University has begun an investigation into its pharmacology department after a professor was accused of not declaring payments for research from companies, including energy drinks manufacturer Red Bull.

Joris Verster published several papers on energy drinks and alcohol in his capacity as associate professor, without disclosing that he was also paid as a consultant for Red Bull and US-based Sen-Jam Pharmaceuticals.

The university does not prohibit consultancy work, but academics are required to disclose any relevant secondary activities when they publish papers under conflict of interest rules.

The investigation follows reports in several Dutch and international media outlets, including Trouw, De Groene Amsterdammer and Investico, that Verster’s research was published without any reference to his paid work for Red Bull and Sen-Jam.

Verster set up a private company, NeuroClinics, for his consultancy work, which frequently overlapped with his academic research.

Hangover pill

He carried out a study into a hangover pill produced by Sen-Jam which concluded, based on a questionnaire circulated around his students, that the medicine did not encourage people to consume more alcohol.

Mariëtte van den Hoven, professor of medical ethics at Amsterdam’s UMC medical centre, said Verster’s methods amounted to a conflict of interest “by using the university to promote your personal goals.”

Another study, published in 2010, concluded that drinking a can of Red Bull improved driving performance, based on observing drivers for four hours in a simulator. It was publicised under the heading “Can Red Bull fuel better driving?”

Verster also published research that disputed claims that mixing energy drinks with alcohol were damaging to people’s health and could lead to aggressive behaviour or unsafe sexual practices.

His conclusion was that combining the drinks meant users consumed less alcohol and were less prone to reckless behaviour.

Sick leave

Verster himself, who has been on sick leave since the start of May, told Trouw he had always been transparent about his private work.

“I have been a consultant for many companies and stated it in all my papers, even when it concerned a minor role,” he said. “I informed Utrecht University about my work as a consultant and the university approved it.”

World.title: Eighth species of American crayfish found in Dutch rivers
World.content:
A new species of crayfish has been found in Dutch rivers, the eighth type to establish itself in the Netherlands after being introduced in the upper Rhine.

The calico crayfish (Faxonius immunis), originally from North America, was spotted in Gelderland by ecologist Pim Lemmers, who first encountered the creatures in a nature reserve near Karlsruhe decades ago.

“I’d been expecting them and looking out for them for a while,” he told NOS. “Last year I found a crayfish pincer and I knew straight away that it might be a significant one.“

The discovery of the pincer, together with the results of DNA samples, are enough to confirm that the crayfish have made it to the Dutch river system.

The water authority in Rivierland has reported the presence of the crayfish to the food standards regulator NVWA, which will in turn notify the European Union, and triggered the protocol for dealing with invasive exotic species.

The Dutch agriculture ministry has set up a working group to investigate how the crayfish can be prevented from spreading. Crayfish damage the local environment by eating indigenous plants and animals and digging in river banks.

“We’re at a very uncertain stage, because are they just in the Klompenwaard area of the Rhine or are they already in our regional waters? Can we keep them out of the waters?” said José Vos, senior policy adviser for the water board.

World.title: Post-Covid fatigue not just caused by inactivity, study finds
World.content:
Patients with post-Covid syndrome suffer muscle damage that cannot be fully be explained by inactivity, research led by scientists at Amsterdam’s Vrije Universiteit (VU) has found.

The team compared the blood and muscle tissue of patients with long Covid and chronic fatigue (ME) with a group of healthy people who spent 60 days in bed as part of a study simulating the effects of space travel.

The post-Covid and ME patients had suffered from energy dips that caused them to avoid exercising or spend long periods in bed, which has a degrading impact on the skeletal muscles.

But the researchers, led by Rob Wüst, a movement scientist at the VU, found differences in the colour of the muscle fibres between the two groups, indicating that the post-Covid patients had a much lower oxygen capacity.

“As skeletal muscle characteristics differ between patients and healthy individuals after bed rest, physical inactivity cannot solely explain the lower exercise capacity and skeletal muscle adaptations in long Covid and ME/CFS patients,” they wrote in a paper published in Nature Communications.

The healthy individuals from the space programme still had bright red fibres, which are still oxygen-rich, while the patients had white fibres, which become exhausted much faster.

Rapid tiredness

The researchers said the difference could explain why post-Covid and ME sufferers become tired so quickly even after modest levels of exercise or exertion. “The redder the fibres, the more stamina a person has,” Wüst explained.

Lung specialist Merel Hellemons, of the Erasmus MC teaching hospital in Rotterdam, told the Volkskrant that the findings were a crucial development in understanding how to treat patients with conditions such as post-Covid syndrome.

“Many patients hear that they need to move more or that being less active is bad for them,” she said.

Wüst said patients should still be encouraged to be more mobile to avoid damage to their muscles, skeletons and cardiovascular system caused by inactivity. “The question is: what is possible? We need more tailored solutions,” he said.

World.title: Profits at KLM up in 2026 despite fuel cost increases
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch airline KLM booked a higher-than-expected profit in the first half of the year, despite the rise in fuel prices caused by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

The company reported revenue of €6.9 bn in the six months to June, an 8% increase compared to the same period last year.

The airline benefited from a decrease in flights from competitors like Qatar Airways and Emirates because of the unrest in the region.

“The measures we are implementing are having a positive impact on our results,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement.

Those measures included passing on higher fuel prices to customers, particularly on long-haul flights.

Yesterday, the Air France-KLM airline group announced they had put in an offer for a stake in Portugal’s TAP airline. Lisbon said last year that it was seeking a major international airline to buy most of the 49.9 percent stake that it planned to sell.

German airline Lufthansa also submitted a bid.

World.title: Man who strangled partner jailed after new forensic method used
World.content:
A man has been convicted of attempting to kill his partner in the first case to use new techniques to detect signs of strangulation in domestic violence.

The 33-year-old man from Rozenburg grabbed the woman by the neck as an argument turned violent last November. Police were alerted by neighbours and pulled the man away from his victim, who later said she was “turning blue”.

She was examined by a medical specialist using a new procedure developed in Rotterdam to gather forensic evidence faster in suspected cases of strangulation.

The doctor said the attack could have been fatal if it was prolonged, a detail that allowed prosecutors to argue that the attack should be classed as attempted manslaughter.

The procedure was introduced last December to try to detect strangulation, which is seen as an early warning sign of femicide, in domestic abuse investigations before the victim’s injuries heal and the evidence disappears.

200 referrals

The medical agency FARR, based in Rotterdam, anticipated receiving 200 inquiries a year, but was called on 150 times in the first three months. In 92% of cases doctors concluded the injuries could have been caused by strangulation. Nine in 10 victims were female and 78% of inquiries were related to domestic violence.

“It’s a huge number,” the agency’s managing director Geranda Zeelenberg told NOS. “Previously we hardly ever saw these people. They were probably always there, but the research we’ve begun has increased awareness of these cases.”

The man from Rozenburg was sentenced to 360 days in prison for attempted manslaughter, including 169 days suspended, and a community service order of 150 hours, in line with the prosecution’s demands.

His lawyer told the court he had no recollection of the events on the night of the attack because he had been taking alcohol and amphetamines, but argued that he had attacked her to try to force her to have sex rather than attempting to kill her.

World.title: Middle East conflict adds to pressure to fill Dutch gas reserves
World.content:
The Netherlands is lagging behind its European partners in filling its gas reserves for the winter, just as a key supplier in the Middle East has announced further restrictions on supplies caused by the conflict between the US and Iran.

QatarEnergy extended “force majeure” restrictions on its LNG cargoes until the end of September, affecting a total of 24 cargoes to European customers.

The company signed a contract to supply up to 3.5 million tonnes of liquified gas to the Netherlands per annum, which came into force this year, but the invocation of force majeure has put this commitment in jeopardy.

The Netherlands’ gas reserves are currently at 36.6% capacity, well below the EU average of 56%.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which triggered a spike in prices, the EU set a target of reaching 90% capacity by November 1. Since then European nations have had to find alternatives to Russian gas.

The Netherlands achieved this level for the first three years, but in 2025 it peaked at just 74% and at the start of April this year the four Dutch storage facilities were at less than 5% capacity.

Energy minister Stientje van Veldhoven said last month she was “confident” that the gas reserves would be filled for the winter, but admitted that the government needed to be “vigilant”.

Demand for gas has also increased during the summer as more consumer and businesses install air conditioning, putting more pressure on energy.

The Dutch government also has agreements to buy gas from Norway and the United States, or could resort to the open market.

The wholesale price of gas on the TTF market, operated by Gasunie, has risen by 50% since mid-June as a result of ongoing attacks by Iran and the US on facilities in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Sitting targets: thieves make off with 88 museum cafe chairs
World.content:

Thieves walked off with all of the chairs from the Bonnefanten Museum café in Maastricht in the early hours of Monday.

Café manager Freek Joosten told local news network L1 that camera footage showed the perpetrators making several trips carrying stacks of chairs at around 4am.

The designer seats are valued at more than €21,000.

The chairs were tied down with iron cables and the grounds are monitored by multiple cameras. The museum has reported the theft to the police.

The museum, which sits on Avenue Céramique in the Limburg capital, specialises in visual arts.

The terrace was recently renovated and the chairs were from designer Fermob Luxembourg. The thieves also took a waste container.

Visitors are still welcome in the café. Joosten has temporarily reallocated the chairs from his catering business to use on the terrace.

Police have asked anyone who saw anything unusual in the vicinity on the night of July 26 to 27, or who may have camera footage, to contact them.

World.title: Water authorities to discuss further drought restrictions
World.content:
Talks are being held in The Hague on Thursday on whether extra measures are needed to conserve drinking water and protect rivers and canals during the ongoing drought.

Water boards, providers of drinking water and the highways agency Rijkswaterstaat are among the agencies attending the discussions at the infrastructure ministry, AD.nl reported.

The Netherlands is currently at level two on a three-stage scale of water shortages, which authorises officials in the ministry to hold crisis talks. An actual crisis is level three.

A spokesman for infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans would not be drawn on the possible outcomes of the meeting, but water boards could agree to bring in further restrictions on river traffic or close sluices.

Key inland routes such as the Twentekanaal, which links three towns in the east of Overijssel, and Deventer’s harbour introduced restrictions this week after the IJssel river dropped to historic low levels.

“By limiting sluice openings we can retain as much fresh water a possible, but these measures have an impact on river traffic and the economy,” the spokesman explained.

Water regulators could introduce one-way traffic on sections of river where the navigable area has narrowed to prevent ships becoming stuck while overtaking, but that will slow down delivery times or force freight to be transported by road.

The flow in the Rhine is down to 650,000 litres per second at Lobith, the point where the river enters the Netherlands – one-third of the normal level for July. Before this year the slowest rate recorded was 782,000 litres per second in the drought year of 1976.

The height of the river is expected to drop to 6.35 metres by the weekend, which would be 15cm below the previous record low.

The Scheldestromen water board in Zeeland issued a ban on Thursday on drawing surface water from ditches, creeks and other waterways to prevent water levels dropping further. The authority warned that the restriction was likely to be in place for a lengthy period of time.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A newly sworn-in judge of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has said he will refuse to sit on the court until four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year, but blocked by the president, are allowed to take their seats. It is the latest development in a months-long dispute between the opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki and the government, which considers the TK to be improperly staffed and therefore illegitimate. Although Nawrocki swore in Sławomir Patyra, who was appointed by the ruling majority in parliament in June, as a TK judge on Tuesday, he continues to refuse to swear in four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year. Po złożeniu przysięgi Patyra ogłosił, że zamierza odmówić orzekania. To gest solidarności z czwórką sędziów, od których prezydent nie chce przyjąć przysięgi https://t.co/jdbKusQ3H9 — OKO.press (@oko_press) July 28, 2026 Shortly after his swearing-in ceremony at the presidential palace on Tuesday, Patyra arrived at the TK headquarters in Warsaw, where he was accompanied by four other judges appointed by parliament this year, including two whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. There, he announced that his decision not to sit on the court was a matter of loyalty to the constitution and his belief in judicial ethos. “I cannot imagine taking an oath today to uphold the constitution, only to start breaking that constitution tomorrow,” he said. Patyra told journalists that he would “submit a declaration of refusal to adjudicate” due to his solidarity with judges who are “unlawfully deprived of the chance to participate in the work of the tribunal”. He added that, along with the other judges chosen this year, he is “fully mobilised to restore the Constitutional Tribunal to its proper, constitutional, systemic form”. Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK, the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, TK’s chief justice Bogdan Święczkowski has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again later in the month, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. After repeated requests, Nawrocki finally decided last week to invite Patyra to the presidential palace. The president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, noted that “there were some doubts” but “the president dispelled them” and added that Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”. Nowo wybrany przez Sejm Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej uchwałą z dnia 11 czerwca 2026 r. sędzia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Sławomir Patyra złożył wobec Prezydenta RP ślubowanie. pic.twitter.com/VLMRAIg1Yj — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. Former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki says that 40 MPs and one senator aligned with him will form their own parliamentary group, deepening a split in the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) after a dispute over party direction and loyalty declarations. The move marks the most serious internal challenge in years to PiS, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023, and follows months of tensions between Morawiecki’s more moderate faction and party conservatives who have pushed the group in a hard-right direction. Once formally established, Morawiecki’s caucus would become the third-largest bloc in the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. Powstanie klub parlamentarny „Rozwój Plus”. Morawiecki zdecydował#PAPInformacjehttps://t.co/IftRdgpIPw — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 29, 2026 One of Morawiecki’s allies, Marcin Horała, told reporters that the creation of the caucus did not mean they were leaving PiS, but “simply setting up a parliamentary group so that we can get on with our work”. He noted, however, that PiS’s parliamentary group “has stopped treating us as its members”. Morawiecki, meanwhile, said that his group remained ready to cooperate with PiS as a “second lung” of the party’s broader political camp, but suggested that the group was moving in a different direction. He said that parts of PiS’s messaging were increasingly influenced by “dissidents and schemers” as well as hardline factions, including Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), a nationalist group that was previously a junior coalition partner of PiS and often clashed with Morawiecki when he was prime minister. Reacting to Morawiecki’s announcement, party chairman Jarosław Kaczyński said the former prime minister had carried out a planned split of the party despite his efforts to reach a deal. “Until the end I made efforts to reach an agreement, unfortunately Mateusz Morawiecki clearly had his own political plan in mind, carried out on the basis of a split in PiS,” Kaczyński wrote on X. The announcement follows a dispute that began after Morawiecki launched his Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) association in April. The former prime minister insisted the association was intended to complement PiS with a pro-development agenda rather than rival it. However, critics within PiS viewed it as an attempt by Morawiecki to build an alternative power base that could eventually evolve into a separate party ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election. Seeking to end the standoff, the party ordered PiS lawmakers to resign from all outside political associations by last Thursday, or face “consequences” including “the loss of membership in PiS”. On Friday, Kaczyński said that “around 30 MPs” had failed to comply and had therefore effectively resigned from the party, adding that Tuesday’s meeting of the party’s political committee would simply confirm this fact. Poland's right-wing opposition PiS party is set to split after a more moderate faction of over 30 MPs loyal to deputy leader @MorawieckiM refused to sign a loyalty pledge demanded by leader @OficjalnyJK, who says that means they have effectively resigned https://t.co/TuqYpGI5ak — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 24, 2026 On Tuesday, the party announced that instead, the committee had referred the cases of 44 members, who either failed to submit the required declarations or submitted them on the wrong form, to the party’s disciplinary officer for individual review, delaying a final decision. “From a formal and legal perspective, Mr Mateusz Morawiecki has not yet been removed from the list of members,” PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek said on Tuesday. PiS disciplinary officer Karol Karski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) he would examine each case individually. “I am open to speaking with each of them so they can present their positions,” Karski said. “At this point, I can initiate proceedings against the individual in question, refer the case to a peer disciplinary tribunal with a motion for punishment – this could include a temporary suspension or expulsion from PiS.” PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, the party has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll at a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. The national-conservative opposition PiS party has named its candidate to be prime minister if it wins next year’s parliamentary elections. Przemysław Czarnek is a hardline conservative who played a prominent role in PiS's campaign against "LGBT ideology" https://t.co/sSJLON00hW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2026 They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Adam Szłapka, the spokesman of the current more liberal government, said Braun was “the ultimate playmaker in this whole game”, who had helped push far-right rhetoric into the political mainstream. “The worst thing about this whole situation is that Poland’s largest opposition party has, in effect, started to adopt Grzegorz Braun’s agenda from A to Z,” Szłapka told broadcaster TVN24. Ostatecznym rozgrywającym w całej tej rozgrywce nie jest ani prezes Jarosław Kaczyński, ani Mateusz Morawiecki, tylko Grzegorz Braun – ocenił w #JedenNaJeden w TVN24 rzecznik rządu Adam Szłapka. World.title: Polish court finds regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage registration unconstitutional
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. Nielegalny Trybunał Konstytucyjny po raz kolejny próbuje zatrzymać państwo, które wykonuje obowiązujące prawo i wyroki europejskich sądów. Transkrypcja zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych jest i będzie legalna. Rozporządzenie, które przyjęliśmy porządkuje dokumenty i… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. World.title: Residents oppose move to add Polish village to list of protected monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. It will help write letters, analyse inquiries from residents, and summarise long documents https://t.co/SLrmVg9VBz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 Earlier this month, Poland’s government approved a resolution enabling the country to participate in the European AI Gigafactory programme, committing more than 400 million zloty towards what the government says would be the largest computing centre in the country’s history. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”.
