The modernization program aims to introduce 7.3 gigawatts (GW) of new and upgraded generating capacity by 2029, with total investment of 6.2 trillion tenge (US$13 billion). Of this amount, 6,484 megawatts (MW) will come from new facilities, while 825 megawatts (MW) will replace outdated capacity.

Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said the program will allow Kazakhstan to fully meet domestic electricity demand starting in early 2027 and achieve a surplus of 1.3 billion kilowatt-hours by the end of the same year.

The planned additions include five gas turbine units at the Zhambyl State District Power Plant with a combined capacity of 210 megawatts (MW) and a combined-cycle facility at the Mangystau Nuclear Power Plant with a capacity of 160 megawatts (MW). A further 4 gigawatts (GW) of capacity is planned for 2028-2029, creating a stable reserve and expanding export potential.

Upgrading networks and improving resilience

The modernization effort also focuses on reducing infrastructure risks. By 2029, Kazakhstan plans to reconstruct 77,500 kilometers of electricity networks and 1,600 kilometers of heating networks. The upgrades are expected to reduce average wear levels of electricity networks from 74% to 45% and heating networks from 52% to 42%, improving reliability and reducing losses.

Several projects have already been completed, including the modernization of the Tekeli energy complex and the launch of a 240 megawatts (MW) combined-cycle power plant in the Kyzylorda Region.

Digitalizing the energy system

Digital transformation is another part of the reform. The Ministry of Energy is developing the EnergyTech platform to integrate data from energy facilities, improve monitoring and increase operational efficiency.

The introduction of smart meters, automated management systems and a cybersecurity center covering more than 200 energy facilities is intended to improve transparency, reduce technical losses and strengthen system security.

Looking ahead

Kazakhstan’s energy modernization reflects a broader challenge faced by many countries: ensuring affordable energy while financing the infrastructure required for long-term reliability.

The success of the program will depend on the timely completion of new-generation projects, the modernization of networks and the ability to improve efficiency without creating excessive pressure on consumers. If implemented as planned, the reforms could strengthen Kazakhstan’s energy security, support industrial growth and increase its role as a regional energy supplier.

World.title: How Kazakhstan Plans to Double Infrastructure Repairs and Improve Energy Reliability
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to significantly expand repairs of its aging energy and utilities infrastructure under a 13 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) national modernization program, with the government aiming to double the pace of network upgrades while increasing the use of domestic manufacturers, officials said at a July 28 government meeting.

Launched at the end of 2024, the National Project on the Modernization of the Energy and Utilities Sectors is designed to reduce the deterioration of engineering infrastructure, improve the reliability of energy supply and public utilities, and strengthen long-term investment in the sector.

Investment and repairs

Deputy Minister of National Economy Assan Darbayev said the project’s institutional framework was completed in 2025 through legislative amendments and the launch of a digital platform overseeing implementation. The project now covers 247 regulated utility companies.

Between 2025 and 2029, Kazakhstan plans to invest 13 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) in the initiative, allocating 6.8 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) to utilities infrastructure and 6.2 trillion tenge (US$13 billion) to the energy sector, according to the Prime Minister’s press service.

The investment is expected to finance the repair and modernization of 84,000 kilometers of engineering networks, add 7,309 megawatts of generating capacity, and build or modernize 27 power generation facilities. By 2029, the government aims to reduce the nationwide average infrastructure wear rate to 40% and cut accident rates by 25%.

Darbayev said financing for the housing and utilities sector has doubled in 2026 compared with the previous year. The government has also secured 625 billion tenge (US$1.3 billion) in financing from six international financial institutions for projects scheduled this year, which officials say will help attract long-term capital while reducing pressure on utility costs.

The government repaired 6,600 kilometers of engineering networks in 2025. This year, it plans to increase that figure to 12,000 kilometers with planned financing of 1.138 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion), marking the project’s transition from institutional preparation to large-scale construction and modernization works.

Improving utility networks

A key objective of the program is improving the financial and operational condition of utility companies operating aging infrastructure.

According to Darbayev, eight utilities were removed from the government’s highest-risk category in 2025, with another eight expected to improve their status this year. By 2029, authorities aim to move 70 utility companies out of the critical-risk category.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said implementation of the national project remains under the personal oversight of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and instructed regional administrations to accelerate modernization efforts. He also directed the National Economy Ministry and other government agencies to ensure the effective use of investment allocated under the program.

Priority for local producers

The modernization program is also expected to boost domestic industrial production.

Minister of Industry and Construction Yersayin Nagaspayev said procurement rules give priority to Kazakh manufacturers. Only companies included in the national register of domestic producers are eligible to participate in project tenders, while procurement is conducted through a dedicated electronic platform designed to give suppliers greater visibility into future demand.

Around 500 domestic manufacturers have been registered as potential suppliers for the national project. According to Nagaspayev, 27 projects are currently in the construction phase, with procurement of construction materials already underway.

Officials said demand for domestically produced equipment and materials under the modernization program is expected to reach approximately 2 trillion tenge (US$4.2 billion) by 2029.

World.title: Tbilisi to demolish landmark Rike Jugs complex
World.content:
The landmark Rike Jugs architectural complex in central Tbilisi, on Europe Square, is being demolished after the city authorities granted permission for the work.

The site, which has remained unused for nearly 15 years, will be redeveloped into a hotel. Most of Rike Park — an area of around 15,000 square metres — will now pass into private ownership.

The complex, known as the Rike Jugs, consists of a music theatre and an exhibition centre. It was built in 2011–2012 in one of the busiest tourist areas of the Georgian capital. The project was conceived by then-President Mikheil Saakashvili and designed by Italian architect Massimiliano Fuksas.

The complex was never used for its intended purpose. Construction was completed just as power changed hands in Georgia, and the new ruling Georgian Dream party took a dim view of the Rike Jugs, along with other architectural projects associated with the Saakashvili era. Party members described the complex as a “dump” and said it was an eyesore.

After years of standing empty, the Rike Jugs were eventually put up for sale. Several auctions failed before the complex was sold in 2022 for 10 million lari (about $3.7 million) to businessman David Khidasheli, an associate of Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili. After Khidasheli’s relationship with the authorities deteriorated — leading to the loss of parts of his business and several licences — he decided to sell the property.

The complex changed hands again in 2025, when it was acquired by Rike Domi, a company registered on 25 April that year.

Under the terms of the deal, the company must build a hotel on the site by 2030, investing 44 million lari (around $16.3 million) in the project.

Urban planning experts and anti-corruption researchers say the sale bears signs of corruption. They argue the complex was sold for well below the market value of comparable property in Tbilisi, particularly in a prime tourist area in the city centre. When it was first offered at auction, the asking price for the Rike Jugs was 95 million lari (about $35.2 million)..

Tbilisi demolishes Rike Jugs complex

World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Five fined and four jailed in Tbilisi activists’ case
World.content:
A court in Georgia has concluded hearings in the cases of 10 activists detained outside Tbilisi City Hall on 26 July. Four were sentenced to administrative detention, while five were fined. Proceedings against one remaining activist have been postponed until 31 July.

What happened

The incident began when activist Tornike Toshkhua staged a solo protest outside Tbilisi City Hall holding a banner reading: “Bidzina d*ck? Yes – No.” The slogan referred to Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Police detained Toshkhua at the scene.

Tornike Toshkhua

In response, a group of activists gathered outside Tbilisi City Hall carrying banners with the same slogan to express solidarity with Toshkhua. Within minutes, police began detaining them as well. In total, nine more people were arrested alongside Toshkhua.

They have been charged with using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders.

Fines and detentions

The activists began appearing in court from the afternoon of 28 July, before the 48-hour detention period had expired.

The first ruling was delivered in the case of Vaso Beridze. The judge fined him 5,000 lari ($1,850), rejecting the Interior Ministry’s request to place him under administrative detention.

In the case of Ia Melitauri, the Interior Ministry sought the maximum administrative detention, but the judge sentenced her to five days in custody instead. Police accused Melitauri of using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders. The judge found no evidence that she had disobeyed police and convicted her only of petty hooliganism.

Melitauri had previously been found guilty twice of administrative offences involving disobeying police and insulting a police officer. A third offence under the same provision carries criminal liability.

According to people present at the hearing, Melitauri told the court she had been mistreated by police following her arrest and showed the judge injuries she said she had sustained during her detention.

The hearing in the case of the third detainee, Tornike Tikaradze, was postponed until 31 July. Tikaradze did not attend the hearing in protest.

Another judge heard the cases of seven other activists and, after several hours of witness testimony and reviewing video evidence, delivered the following verdicts:

Tornike Toshkhua was fined 3,000 lari ($1,110);

Mariam Mekantsishvili was fined 6,000 lari ($2,220);

Nato Bolkvadze was sentenced to five days of administrative detention;

Shako Bagdoshvili was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Lasha Dgebuadze was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Marine Nanava was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850);

Sandro Sekhniashvili was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850).

Scuffle outside the courthouse

Several reports of scuffles between members of the public and court bailiffs emerged throughout the day as the hearings were under way.

Videos circulating on social media showed bailiffs forcibly removing people from the courthouse.

During the final hearing, activist Ruska Mchedlidze and lawyer Marika Arevadze said court bailiffs used force against them.

Ruska Mchedlidze

“Zonder bailiff Davit Matiashvili and other zonder bailiffs physically assaulted me in the courtyard of this unjust court. Yes, I spat at them, and yes, I spat at them again after the assault, once I was outside the gates.

These bruises will heal, but everyone will remember his disgrace forever. His, and that of the other zonder bailiffs carrying out unlawful orders. There were around 20 police officers standing there, watching as these aggressive men assaulted me, and not one of them intervened,” Mchedlidze wrote on social media.

Activist Lado Jakhua also shared footage showing several court bailiffs dragging Ruska Mchedlidze out of the courthouse courtyard.

Tbilisi activists sentenced over protest

World.title: Opposition grows in Abkhazia over monument to citizens killed in Ukraine war
World.content:
A group of Abkhaz politicians and public figures has spoken out against plans to erect a monument in Sukhum to citizens of Abkhazia who were killed while fighting in the war in Ukraine.

They appealed to the republic’s president, Badra Gunba, and the city authorities to cancel or postpone the decision, which was approved by the Sukhum City Assembly at the initiative of the city administration.

The appeal was signed by former parliament speaker Valery Kvarchia, People’s Artist Batal Jopua, historian Guram Gumba, former education minister Adgur Kakoba, Akhyatsa civic organisation head Akhra Bzhania, and former leader of the Aruaa veterans’ movement Ilya Guniya.

The signatories argue that any memorial erected in the Abkhaz capital should commemorate historical events only after they have stood the test of time.

“Fighting is still under way, people are dying, yet the local authorities in Abkhazia have taken the unprecedented decision to erect a monument to a war that has not yet ended.

“No one knows how, when or on what terms these two closely related peoples will first reach understanding and then reconciliation. But that will inevitably happen. Only then, years later, will we be able to return to the question of creating a memorial to this historical event,” the appeal says.

The authors also point out that Sukhum still has no monuments to Abkhazia’s first president, Vladislav Ardzinba, or to volunteers from the North Caucasus republics who fought alongside Abkhazia during the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war.

“If we intend to begin preserving our historical memory, we should start with them. Otherwise, not only the people of Abkhazia but also our friends in the North Caucasus and the parents of the fallen volunteers will not understand us,” the appeal says.

The signatories also argue that the issue has an important foreign policy dimension. Despite its strategic partnership with Russia, they say, Abkhazia is not at war with Ukraine.

“Our state has never carried out any mobilisation or organisational measures in connection with what Russia calls its ‘special military operation’. The relevant authorities have no information about either the total number of our citizens in the conflict zone or the terms under which they entered military service,” the appeal says.

They argue that officially recognising the participation of Abkhaz citizens in the fighting would provide diplomatic grounds for Ukraine and its regional allies, including Turkey, to regard Abkhazia as a party to the conflict. As a result, they say, “our citizens’ participation in the war would cease to be a matter of personal choice and instead become our collective choice.”

Although the appeal has been signed by only six people, its authors say they believe their views are widely shared across Abkhaz society.

“We are in contact with people from all walks of life and can say with confidence that thousands of residents of Sukhum and citizens of Abkhazia share our views and the arguments set out above.”

The signatories call on the president and the city authorities to act with prudence and wisdom.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Monument to Abkhazians who fought in Ukraine

World.title: Turkey takes practical steps to restore rail link with Armenia
World.content:
Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

Turkey has begun restoring the entire railway infrastructure along the Akyaka–Gyumri route, the section connecting it with Armenia. Preliminary estimates suggest the work will take two to three months to complete. Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas told this to a group of Armenian journalists visiting Turkey.

According to Toptas, the construction work now under way in Turkey signals preparations for reopening the Armenian-Turkish border. He said reopening the border would give Turkey another route to the Caucasus. It would also allow Armenia to establish transport links with Middle Eastern countries through Turkey.

Kadir Bozan, chairman of the Kars Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also told the Armenian journalists that freight traffic on the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway has increased by 400% in recent months. He did not specify whether Armenia uses the route for exports or imports.

However, on 24 May, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that “the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway is now open for exports from Armenia and imports into Armenia.” He described the development as extremely important for the country’s economy.

Armenian journalists’ impressions from their visit to Turkey

According to official information, a group of Armenian journalists travelled to Turkey as part of a journalist exchange programme. The purpose of the visit was to observe progress on the work to reopen the railway on the Turkish side.

The journalists also wanted to see how Turkey’s railway infrastructure operates more broadly. In particular, they travelled by train from Kars to Akyaka. The 57-kilometre journey took just 50 minutes.

After returning, they wrote that Akyaka station lies only 18–20 kilometres from the Armenian city of Gyumri. That means the journey would take just 30–40 minutes. However, the closed border currently makes it impossible to travel from Akyaka to Gyumri.

Tender announced for Akyaka–Gyumri highway

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas said Turkey plans to restore not only the railway but also the highway.

“The tender for the construction of the road from Akyaka to Gyumri has already been announced. We now expect work on that project to begin as well,” he said.

According to Toptas, these developments indicate that both governments are moving towards establishing good-neighbourly and friendly relations.

The mayor said reopening the Armenian-Turkish border and expanding bilateral economic cooperation would benefit both countries. He believes the two sides have opportunities to cooperate in both agriculture and industry.

The Armenian journalists also spoke with residents of Turkish settlements near the Armenian border. Most said they hope the border will reopen as soon as possible. They also believe it will create new economic opportunities for local communities on both sides of the border.

“We do not expect any obstacles to reopening the border”

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas expressed optimism about the prospects for normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey. In his view, once Armenia and Azerbaijan normalise their relations, reopening the Armenian-Turkish border should not present any difficulties.

He said that, on the instructions of the Turkish president and under the coordination of the transport ministry, officials have begun preparatory work at the border crossing points ahead of the border’s reopening. Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: A blessing for some, tailwinds feel like a near-death experience in hurdles
World.content:
After rain blighted the first six days of the Commonwealth Games, Glasgow dialled up the dimmer on Thursday morning.

But a gorgeous, sunny, slightly brisk morning turned blustery and bleak by the time athletics competition was in full swing at Scotstoun Stadium.

It mercifully stayed dry as day seven's heats and qualifiers kicked off, but the wind was wreaking havoc across the track and field.

Australian javelin thrower Cameron McEntyre was launching into a mighty headwind that saw none of the 17 throwers reach the qualification standard of 84 metres.

The temperature plummeted as clouds rolled over Scotstoun. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McEntyre got through on his 78.91m effort, but Kenya's Julius Yego, boasting the fourth longest throw in the Commonwealth this year, missed out on qualifying for the final as he finished in 13th spot.

"Everyone struggled with the wind and the temperature as well. Hopefully better conditions tomorrow and then push for a podium [but] everyone's in the same boat," McEntyre said, crediting his thorough preparation at training for keeping him ready for a day like today.

"If it's pissing down with rain or huge headwinds, whatever the conditions are, we just deal with it because we know one day there's gonna be a competition that's exactly the same."

And while hurling a spear into a breeze that's trying to throw it back at you might sound like the more dangerous prospect, Michelle Jenneke said her 100m hurdles with the wind at her back is a frightening experience.

Michelle Jenneke said the tailwind can mess up hurdlers' all-important stride patterns. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I get pretty jealous when I see the sprinters because you get a tailwind and you run fast, we get a tailwind and we're like 'let's try not to die today'. The hurdles were really coming at us," Jenneke said.

"I am just really really grateful we knew that was going to be a possibility and we really trained for it. It was tough today, towards the end I was really struggling to make sure I was hitting my stride pattern. But I think I did it really well, I did really safe and still managed to run quite fast."

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

Jenneke clocked a time of 12.72 seconds, 0.05 of a second outside her personal best from two years ago, but this time with an illegal +4.3 metres per second tailwind.

"The wind was really pushing us onto the hurdles, it was a good time, though," she said after progressing to the evening's final as the sixth-fastest qualifier.

"Hopefully a little less windy [in the final] but I did really prepare for that tailwind and I think I handled it better than some of the other athletes."

Adeyah Brewster (background) went down at the final hurdle. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She certainly did, with Barbados's Adeyah Brewster clipping the final hurdle and falling flat on her belly barely 6 metres short of the finish line.

National 400m champion Reece Holder experienced both sides of the coin in his single-lap semifinal, saying it was exactly what they expected when coming to Glasgow.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

"Everyone's running in the same conditions, so can't really complain because everyone's showing up to show out," he said.

Holder, who suffered a hamstring injury in mid-May, missed the 400m final while teammate Tom Reynolds won his semifinal to progress.

"I actually only just put spikes on two weeks ago from May," he said.

"So to come out here and run 45s, just be thankful for that and push forward for the future.

"I just don't think I'm race fit. Big ups to everyone else out there putting on a show for everyone in these conditions, but I just don't think I was there."

World.title: Parents of Australian facing possible death penalty in Syria question confession
World.content:
The family of a Gold Coast man facing a possible death penalty for allegedly murdering another Australian in Syria has gone public to express frustration at the lack of progress made by the federal government in the case.

Patrick Stevenson, 20, has been detained for nearly seven months in north-western Syria accused of the shooting murder of Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess, 40, from northern New South Wales.

Mr Stevenson's mother, Angela Bell, said Australian officials had told her diplomatic efforts had gone nowhere.

She told the ABC she was disappointed by her dealings with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT).

Patrick Stevenson travelled to Syria late last year. (Supplied)

"They say … that their policy is that he shouldn't have been travelling to Syria … and that's where the conversation gets stuck," she told the ABC's 7.30 program.

"They use the word 'limited' a lot. They don't use the word failure, but basically the sense is they … have limited capacity to help in this situation."

The ABC has established that Mr Burgess was a tree lopper from the village of Eltham, near Lismore, who spent months in Afghanistan before settling in Syria last year with his Australian wife and their daughters.

Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess was shot dead in the town of Darkush on December 31, 2025. (Supplied)

According to Syrian authorities, Mr Burgess was shot dead in his home in the town of Darkush in Idlib province on December 31, while his wife and daughters were in another room.

Mr Stevenson was arrested nearby soon afterwards and later charged with premeditated murder, an offence punishable by death in Syria.

Syrian authorities allege he confessed to firing at least eight shots from an AK-47 at Mr Burgess.

But his family and Australian legal team say they do not know how the alleged confession was obtained and have raised serious concerns about whether he will receive a fair trial.

"Not a single document has come from Syria explaining the charges," Ms Bell said.

"There's no paperwork, there's no access to Patrick."

No Australian government representative has visited Mr Stevenson in prison, attended his court hearings or independently assessed his welfare.

Clay Stevenson says his son's health has deteriorated severely. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

Last week, Mr Stevenson's father, Clay, travelled to Syria carrying his son's Australian medical records and a psychiatric report for the court.

He visited Mr Stevenson in Sarmada prison and attended a court hearing on Sunday — the first time a member of the family had seen him since he secretly left Australia last October.

His parents say his mental health has deteriorated severely in detention.

Mr Stevenson has learning disorders, ADHD and probable autism spectrum disorder, according to a 2025 psychiatric report.

He travelled to Syria late last year and came to the attention of counterterrorism police after becoming radicalised, an ABC investigation has established.

Do you know more? Contact Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop on Signal: @seanrdunlop.01 and on Protonmail: seanrdunlop@protonmail.com

on Signal: and on Protonmail: Please use this form to get in contact with the ABC Investigations team, or if you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

The family's Australian lawyer, Bernadette Zaydan, said the alleged confession raised "alarm bells" because it was unclear how it had been obtained.

"Was it given under duress? Was it given in writing? Was it given orally?" she said.

"We have grave concerns for his welfare."

Ms Zaydan urged the federal government to press for Mr Stevenson to receive a transparent trial before an independent court, rather than one associated with Syria's administration or armed forces.

Canberra struggling to gain access

The ABC understands Australia has made representations about Mr Stevenson's case, but DFAT told his family last month that the Syrian government had shown little engagement.

Correspondence seen by the ABC shows the department repeatedly told the family it could not obtain information from Syrian authorities and had no access to the country's detention facilities.

Australia has no embassy or consulate in Syria, severely limiting the consular assistance it can provide.

Canberra has also been unable to independently monitor the investigation into Mr Burgess's death.

After the ABC revealed the case, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that Australia was providing support to both families.

"Legal processes will take their course overseas, of course, and that is appropriate," he said.

"I feel for the family of the person who's lost their life, and we're connected to them and providing support for them.

"We're also providing support for the family of the man who's been charged."

But Canberra has struggled to establish relations with Syria's new government, unlike allies including the United States and France.

Australia continues to impose sanctions on Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the militant group from which Syria's new leadership emerged, and lists it as a terrorist organisation.

The group, which formally dissolved last year, was previously affiliated with Al Qaeda.

Parents discovered police were investigating son

Mr Stevenson left Australia on a flight to Bali on October 10 before travelling to Syria.

His parents said they had no idea he had left the country.

"I was shocked to find out that he was there," Clay Stevenson said.

"It's just like, 'Wow, what's going through his head to be in Syria and who helped him get there?'"

Patrick Stevenson's parents said he told them he intended to study at a Syrian university and hoped to find a wife.

They tried desperately to convince him to return home.

Patrick Stevenson is facing a possible death penalty in Syria. (Supplied)

The family said they discovered he was overseas only after officers from the Queensland Police Security and Counter-Terrorism Command contacted them.

His parents said officers searched his bedroom at his father's home and questioned them about extremist material he had allegedly posted in a group chat.

"He was talking to someone in a group chat that the Australian government were investigating and Patrick had come up as peripheral to another investigation," Ms Bell said.

She said ASIO later questioned her about her son's associations on the Gold Coast.

Mr Stevenson converted to Islam during his final year of high school in 2023, according to his family.

Patrick Stevenson converted to Islam in his final year of high school in 2023. (Supplied)

By last year, he was showing signs of radicalisation, including sharing speeches by Anwar al-Awlaki, the US-born Al Qaeda cleric and propagandist killed in a US drone strike in Yemen in 2011.

He also volunteered with Muslim Youth GC (MYGC), a youth group connected to the Worongary Mosque on the Gold Coast.

The group's leader, Abdul Rahman Nasiri, said neither it nor any other local organisation had supported Mr Stevenson's journey and he was free to make his own choices.

"We created MYGC to help young people [both Muslim and non-Muslim] steer away and overcome the negative challenges they face daily and give them the correct understanding of Islam, free from the stereotypes and misinformation that can appear online or in the media," he said in a written statement.

Case referred to civilian court

DFAT advised Mr Stevenson's family that Syrian authorities initially treated the shooting as an accident.

They later investigated whether he was affiliated with the Islamic State terrorist group.

According to information provided to the family, that investigation ended in February when authorities referred the case to the civilian criminal courts as a murder prosecution, rather than as a terrorism case.

The prosecution is likely to test Syria's fractured legal system as the country attempts to rebuild its institutions after 14 years of civil war.

Syrian legal sources told the ABC that it could take up to a year for the court to reach a verdict.

Any death sentence imposed by an ordinary criminal court would have to be reviewed by the Court of Cassation, considered by a clemency committee and approved by Syria's president before it could be carried out.

Patrick Stevenson travelled to Syria late last year. (Supplied)

Quiet man who avoided the camera

Those who knew Mr Burgess described him as quiet, devout and reluctant to be photographed.

"He was a very soft-spoken, gentle sort of guy," said Shahz Rana, a former president of the North Coast Muslim Association.

"Not too talkative, just used to keep to himself, but was still nice and polite to others."

Mr Rana said the news of his death had shocked the community.

"It was a little bit surprising that he was in Syria, but it was shocking news and I feel sad for him," he said.

Mr Rana said Mr Burgess told community members in about 2024 that his family was moving to Malaysia to live in a Muslim community and learn more about the faith.

He was unaware the family had spent at least six months travelling through Taliban-ruled Afghanistan before moving to Darkush, near Syria's border with Türkiye.

It is not known what brought the family to Syria. The ABC does not suggest they had links to extremist groups.

People who knew the two men said Mr Burgess took Mr Stevenson under his wing and that they became close before the shooting.

Widow could spare Stevenson's life

Mr Stevenson's fate may ultimately rest with a third Australian: Mr Burgess's widow, Amatullah Laurie Duniam.

Under the Syrian legal system, she could spare him execution by granting forgiveness, potentially in exchange for a payment of blood money, known as diya.

Ms Duniam and other members of Mr Burgess's family declined to speak to the ABC.

World.title: 'Take them seriously': CFMEU administrator on Setka threats
World.content:
CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby has opened up on threats from John Setka, cast doubt on a statement made by former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan and questioned the value of royal commissions during an extensive 7.30 interview.

Mr Crosby was appointed to the role in May following the resignation of its previous administrator, Mark Irving.

At the time, Mr Crosby said he was committed to changing the culture of the union, which in 2024 was placed into administration by the Albanese government following revelations it had been infiltrated by organised crime.

Mr Irving had said he had received death threats during his tenure.

Mr Crosby says he too has received threats, a first for him, from former CFMEU boss John Setka.

"I take them seriously," Mr Crosby told 7.30.

"There's not much I can do about it. The police have taken out the Victorian equivalent of an AVO.

"I'm basically ignoring it and moving on.

"I think about the work that we're doing in this union, [and] I'm incredibly proud of the people who have come into this union to reform it."

John Setka is accused of threatenig CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby. (AAP: Stefan Postles)

Asked if he would take a meeting with Mick Gatto, who had wanted one with his predecessor, Mr Crosby said he would not.

"Why would I associate with anybody like that and give him credibility?" Mr Crosby said.

Mr Crosby said in his view the union had done well to weed out corruption since it went into administration, telling 7.30 that he believed criminal elements no longer held sway.

"They have very little grip on the union," Mr Crosby said.

"We've moved off 27 leaders, 150 staff members of various kinds have gone away. We've got a whole new team in there rebuilding that union from the ground up."

Scepticism on royal commission

With corruption and criminality having been major problems for the CFMEU, Mr Crosby was adamant that corruption had also been responsible for a blowout in costs on major Victorian projects.

The CFMEU is being rebuilt "from the ground up", Michael Crosby says. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

That was something former premier Jacinta Allan had refused to admit, when she blamed inflation rather than CFMEU corruption for the skyrocketing costs on Victoria's Big Build.

"That's difficult to accept," Mr Crosby told 7.30.

Mr Crosby said criminality had generally caused the cost of construction in Australia to be more expensive.

"Inevitably … somebody is clipping the ticket on the way through," he said.

Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan blamed cost blow outs on Victoria's Big Build on inflation. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"Some of the corruption is about who gets to do the work, and these are rich contracts because they're big projects.

"If you can get that job, then you get paid by the government to do that."

Mr Crosby said that process was a major problem for the construction industry to reckon with.

"Criminality comes out of the way in which the industry is organised," he said.

"Governments hand over control of a particular infrastructure project to a head contractor, the head contractor then hands over control to subcontractors, and then they get labour hire agencies in.

"Right through that, that's where supervision breaks down, and you get these criminals coming in, subverting the union, corrupting the union and its leadership, but lining their pockets all the way through."

New Victorian premier Ben Carroll has called a royal commission into the construction sector in the state. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A major question for any royal commission into construction, as called for by new Victorian Premier Ben Carroll, is if it can fix the major issues around corruption in the sector.

It is something that Mr Crosby is unsure of.

"Will [we] cooperate with the royal commission? Absolutely," he said.

"I am sceptical about royal commissions. There's been four into the CFMEU [and] they've all failed."

World.title: Toy library makes statement grieving loss of Helena Wright and children
World.content:
A South Australian toy library has expressed sadness following the deaths of a mother and her two children, which police are treating as a murder-suicide.

The bodies of Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were retrieved from waters off Cape Northumberland in SA's south-east on Monday.

The search for her three-month-old son was formally called off by South Australian Police on Wednesday afternoon, after receiving advice the child could not have survived.

Ms Wright was a volunteer committee member at the Mount Gambier Toy Library, which issued a statement on Thursday.

"Mt Gambier Toy Library is deeply saddened by the tragic loss of a member of our committee and her children. Our thoughts are with their family, friends and everyone affected by this devastating event," it said. "Our volunteer committee and toy library community are grieving and supporting one another."

Police on Wednesday confirmed Ms Wright had attended a local police station on Sunday and officers had attended her home to conduct a welfare check on Monday morning following a call from a friend. Her car was found later that morning at Cape Northumberland.

The three deaths have shaken the Port MacDonnell community, which has rallied around locals who volunteered to help the police search.

The matter is now the subject of a coronial investigation.

World.title: Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years
World.content:
Sydney Roosters sent a warning to the rest of the NRL about their premiership credentials with a 82-12 whipping of North Queensland in Townsville, the most points by a winning team in 91 years.

Halfback Sam Walker, in the midst of a multi-million dollar contract negotiation, showed why Roosters supremo Nick Politis wants to keep him at the club for life in a masterclass display.

This was a muscle flex of epic proportions as the visitors scored the equal most first half points in premiership history to lead 48-6 after 40 minutes.

The Roosters scored eight first half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker's 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at halftime with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

North Queensland were helpless before the Tricolour onslaught. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock )

The Roosters temporarily joined Penrith on 34 competition points at the top of the table in their most complete performance of the season.

It was their sixth win in a row and a sign that come September they will be in prime position to challenge their bogey team Penrith.

The Cowboys are hanging on in eighth position but will drop back to ninth if Canterbury beat Melbourne away on Friday night.

The nature of the thrashing will test Cowboys coach Todd Payten's ability to get an appropriate response

Captain Tedesco, fresh from a hat-trick of tries last week, started and finished the opening try and it was carnage from that moment.

Roosters forwards Naufahu Whyte and Salesi Foketi monstered the hosts early and the spine of Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Walker and Reece Robson ran riot.

Tedesco, also the NSW custodian, is making a compelling case to oust Reece Walsh from the fullback position for Australia at the World Cup later in the year.

The Cowboys levelled at six-all when halves Jake Clifford and Jaxon Purdue combined to put Braidon Burns over but that was the only moment the match was in the balance.

A brilliant interchange of passing between halfback Walker and Tedesco led to the No.7 slicing over.

Tedesco then laid on a try for centre Hugo Savala with a left-foot grubber and it was clear which way the match was heading. . Walker's left foot step on the last tackle to score his second was elite.

The dazzling half set up runaway Foketi for a 40m rampage to the line.

The last try of the match, scored by replacement fullback Cody Ramsey, featured Walker grubbering and then kicking the ball over the head of the last dismal line of Cowboys defence.

AAP

World.title: 'Sadness' falls across coastal community after double murder-suicide
World.content:
Residents of a South Australian coastal town rocked by a double murder-suicide say a "sadness" has fallen across the tight-knit community.

Helena Wright, 36, and her 23-month-old daughter were pulled from the ocean near Port MacDonnell on Monday, with Ms Wright's two-month-old son still missing.

Helicopters and planes flew over the scene on Monday while boats scoured the ocean nearby searching for the boy.

Weather hampered search efforts on Tuesday and Wednesday, limiting searchers to foot patrols along the coastline.

Police made the call to end the formal search for the baby boy as of Wednesday afternoon, saying he could not have survived almost three days in the conditions.

Police are treating the death of Helena Wright and her two children as a murder-suicide. (Supplied)

Also on Wednesday, police said Ms Wright had attended a local police station the day before the deaths.

Police conducted a welfare check at her home at Compton, near Mount Gambier, just hours before the public found Ms Wright's vehicle running near the cliffs at Cape Northumberland.

Country Fire Service Kingsley Group officer Grant Fensom's team is based in Port MacDonnell, and he helped with rescue efforts.

He said volunteers told police the best chance of finding Ms Wright and her children was on Monday during the more favourable weather conditions.

"The locals, let alone the SES and the police, did their absolute best to locate them on the first day, which obviously you know resulted in two people being found and not the third," Mr Fensom said.

"The last two days it has been hard, been wet, it's been windy, and the sea has definitely been rough.

Police say they are continuing to search for the missing baby boy. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

" So it's been a trying time knowing that you can't get out there and actually probably continue a search to give some closure to some people. "

Mr Fensom said the incident was hard on a town that prided itself on being welcoming.

"So to have something happen in our town is hard because people want to think that they can always help someone out that's in need," he said.

Strength in speaking up

Salt cafe owner Mel Lewis donated more than 30 meals to those on the ground as police and SES volunteers from around the state descended on Port MacDonnell to aid the search.

Mel Lewis says the deaths have taken a toll on the tight-knit town. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

She said the entire town felt a "sadness".

"People are coming together, maybe connecting a little bit more, reaching out to family, friends, hugging their children a little bit tighter," she said.

Ms Lewis said it was important the town took the time to support one another.

"It shows more strength to reach out and ask for help than to not," she said.

"I know personally to do that, and it is very, very tough, but we have a lot of services around for us to be able to reach out.

"But even just your friends and your family, but like I said, it just shows so much more strength asking for help than not."

Emergency services volunteer Roger Bobolka said the impact spread beyond those on the ground aiding the search effort.

Roger Bobulka said the incident would "stick" with locals. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"You can talk to anyone in town now and you can tell they've been impacted in some way because it's not the sort of thing you can just shut off and push aside and move on," he said.

"It's the sort of thing that hangs around for quite some time and it will for the community.

"I mean it's happened in a fairly prominent location within Port MacDonnell, so you can't get away from it."

Shoreline monitoring continues

Police Commissioner Grant Stevens told 891 ABC Adelaide officers would continue to monitor the shoreline for the missing baby boy despite ceasing the formal search.

"We will continue searching the shoreline in the coming days in the hope of being able to recover the little infant, but we're not holding a lot of hope in that regard," he said.

He said the deaths of children were "distressing" not only for police but for the community.

Commissioner Grant Stevens says the incident is distressing. (ABC News)

"It's heartbreaking to think we can't find the little infant, that sits heavily on the shoulders of the people involved, and it's not just police," he said.

The bodies of Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were recovered from the ocean. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

The commissioner added the case was now part of a coronial investigation and would not elaborate on any interactions Ms Wright had with police.

"That evidence [to the coroner] will include all of the activities involving Helena and her interactions with police, any other services in the days leading up to what we are now describing as a murder-suicide," he said.

World.title: Nauru officially changes name to Naoero
World.content:
Nauru has officially changed its name to Naoero, the Micronesian nation's government has announced.

A constitutional amendment to rename the country passed parliament in May, following a proposal tabled by President David Adeang in January.

Mr Adeang said at the time that the name Nauru had been recognised internationally since the island's independence, the proposed change sought to "more faithfully honour our nation's heritage, our language, and our identity".

However, a national referendum was expected to follow to complete the constitutional procedures.

"The Republic of Naoero is the new official designation for what was previously known as Nauru. The abbreviated form will be Naoero, with the code updated to NRO, and the people will be referred to as dei-Naoero," the government said in a statement.

Nauru's parliament passed a constitutional amendment to change the name in May. (AFP: Mike Leyral)

It added that Mr Adeang delivered his opening message to parliament on July 20 and addressed the decision to return the country to its traditional name, Naoero, "following extensive discussions".

"The decision not to pursue a referendum was reached after thoughtful deliberation that Naoero is not a new name seeking acceptance by the people.

"It is already the identity of the people, is on the national coat of arms, and spoken in the community; and importantly is allowed by the Constitution.

"While a referendum is intended to determine the will of the people, the name Naoero has never been lost, but rather waiting to be fully embraced."

The government said a bill to amend the constitution to allow the name change was tabled in January. It was followed by a layover period of 90 days and the unanimous vote in favour by the members of parliament.

Speaker Marcus Stephen certified the amendment on May 13 to enact the name change.

"International organisations and countries have formally been notified of the change and have begun making the transition," the government statement said.

"Naoero is the beginning of renewed national pride, and a new chapter founded on unity, responsibility, patriotism, better health, education, and sustainable development.

" The future of Naoero will be built by learning from the mistakes of the past and using their experience to make wiser decisions for the generations to come. "

The United Nations said Nauru had informed it about changing its name to Republic of Naoero on June 26.

This story was first published on rnz.co.nz

World.title: Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts Matthew Knott July 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Up to 400 Defence Force personnel will be tracked during weapons training as part of a sophisticated study that follows years of growing complaints about a lack of action on alarming reports of blast injuries among military veterans. In the first-of-its-kind study, researchers will cross-reference blast pressure readings from gauges on soldiers’ helmets with blood tests and neurological data conducted within a day of exposure to blasts. Retired lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan, an advocate for action on blast injuries in defence, during his time in the army. Blood tests analysed at Monash University’s Melbourne laboratory will be used to detect tiny amounts of proteins known to be released in the bloodstream during a traumatic brain injury. The study is a response to the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which recommended the government establish a brain injury program to better understand the impact of repetitive low-level blast exposure on brain processes.



Retired army lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan has led a veterans’ push for greater action from government and the Australian Defence Force on brain injuries among current and former service personnel. “From Afghanistan, there are guys now from that who have committed suicide,” Scanlan previously told this masthead. “And not just suicides. Families are being destroyed because of the effect it’s having. I think they deserve a lot better.” Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said: “The health, safety and wellbeing of current and former serving Defence Force personnel is my highest priority. “As part of our response to the royal commission, we’ve been investing in research and monitoring to better understand the complex nature of brain injury and its causes.



“While a co-ordinated effort is under way to decrease risks where possible, in line with international research, we know we need to do more.” In a 2024 interview with this masthead, then-army chief Simon Stuart apologised to veterans suffering from potentially avoidable impacts of blast trauma. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations The blasts, the battle and at last an apology. Now it’s time for action “There have been research and trials and other work going on since 2010, so far as I can ascertain. I think what’s been missing is sort of the golden thread of logic,” he said. Previous ADF studies have recorded blast pressure via the helmet-mounted gauges, but have not cross-referenced the results with blood and neurological data to determine the actual effect of blast pressure in real time.



Professor Sandy Shultz, a principal investigator at Monash’s school of translational medicine, said: “There has been very little research on brain injury as a result of low-level blast exposure, despite this being such a common experience across the defence sector. “Exactly how and to what extent low-level and repetitive exposures to blast affects the brain is really unknown. “The knowledge gained from this research will help inform policy and guidelines around what thresholds can result in a brain injury and when ADF personnel should be removed from further exposure.” The study, which will be conducted over the next four years, will focus on how repeated, low-level blast exposures may impact brain health across a military career. More is known about high-level blast events, which can result in immediate traumatic brain injury.



The study will focus initially on the army but could later be extended to the navy and air force. “By combining blast monitoring, blood-based biomarkers and cognitive and psychometric assessments, we’re building the evidence needed to strengthen force health protection,” said army neurologist Lieutenant Colonel Antony Sutherland, a member of the study team. The royal commission, released in 2024, found that traumatic brain injuries are associated with a heightened risk of death by suicide in veteran and civilian populations. “Traumatic brain injury from blast exposure is common in active-duty military personnel,” the final report found. “Many researchers believe that the pressure wave passing through the brain significantly disrupts brain function, causing damage.”



The royal commission found current and ex-service members “reported receiving insufficient support from the ADF for brain injury and having difficulty obtaining compensation”. If you are a current or former ADF member or a relative and need counselling or support, contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046. World.title: Launching a myth
World.content:
“When, as one does, fact checking Homer’s Odyssey, I find that 1196 ships sailed to Troy. Helen, the face that launched 1196 ships doesn’t have the same ring,” reckons Jane Stranger of Erskineville. “Clearly the PR gurus and brand managers of the time thought so, too.”

Barry Lamb of Eastwood’s suggested names for the Australian Underwater Hockey team (C8) are so elite that they could utilise any of them. Take your pick from, The Scubaroos, The Flipperoos, The Scudding Neptunes or The Munned Stullets.

Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls suggests The Hockeyrays, though that could result in a complaint from the Australian women’s water polo team, The Stingers.

“Your correspondent found the film Jedda traumatising as a young child,” notes Mary Julian of Glebe. “I was also at the opening in 1959 and was probably fearful, too, but I managed another look at the movie recently. What amazed me were the perfect English accents, dubbed, for all indigenous and non-indigenous actors, except, of course Chips Rafferty. Chips used his own Aussie voice.”

Speaking of Australian cinema, Nola Tucker of Kiama thinks there’s one film that could perform another type of screening: “My Japanese grandson-in-law, Yuji, used to assess possible new friends by their attitude to The Castle [SMH, July 29]. Like the film, and they’re fine; don’t like it, not welcome. Seems a good enough standard to go by.”

World.title: Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts Matthew Knott July 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Up to 400 Defence Force personnel will be tracked during weapons training as part of a sophisticated study that follows years of growing complaints about a lack of action on alarming reports of blast injuries among military veterans. In the first-of-its-kind study, researchers will cross-reference blast pressure readings from gauges on soldiers’ helmets with blood tests and neurological data conducted within a day of exposure to blasts. Retired lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan, an advocate for action on blast injuries in defence, during his time in the army. Blood tests analysed at Monash University’s Melbourne laboratory will be used to detect tiny amounts of proteins known to be released in the bloodstream during a traumatic brain injury. The study is a response to the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which recommended the government establish a brain injury program to better understand the impact of repetitive low-level blast exposure on brain processes.



Retired army lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan has led a veterans’ push for greater action from government and the Australian Defence Force on brain injuries among current and former service personnel. “From Afghanistan, there are guys now from that who have committed suicide,” Scanlan previously told this masthead. “And not just suicides. Families are being destroyed because of the effect it’s having. I think they deserve a lot better.” Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said: “The health, safety and wellbeing of current and former serving Defence Force personnel is my highest priority. “As part of our response to the royal commission, we’ve been investing in research and monitoring to better understand the complex nature of brain injury and its causes.



“While a co-ordinated effort is under way to decrease risks where possible, in line with international research, we know we need to do more.” In a 2024 interview with this masthead, then-army chief Simon Stuart apologised to veterans suffering from potentially avoidable impacts of blast trauma. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations The blasts, the battle and at last an apology. Now it’s time for action “There have been research and trials and other work going on since 2010, so far as I can ascertain. I think what’s been missing is sort of the golden thread of logic,” he said. Previous ADF studies have recorded blast pressure via the helmet-mounted gauges, but have not cross-referenced the results with blood and neurological data to determine the actual effect of blast pressure in real time.



Professor Sandy Shultz, a principal investigator at Monash’s school of translational medicine, said: “There has been very little research on brain injury as a result of low-level blast exposure, despite this being such a common experience across the defence sector. “Exactly how and to what extent low-level and repetitive exposures to blast affects the brain is really unknown. “The knowledge gained from this research will help inform policy and guidelines around what thresholds can result in a brain injury and when ADF personnel should be removed from further exposure.” The study, which will be conducted over the next four years, will focus on how repeated, low-level blast exposures may impact brain health across a military career. More is known about high-level blast events, which can result in immediate traumatic brain injury.



The study will focus initially on the army but could later be extended to the navy and air force. “By combining blast monitoring, blood-based biomarkers and cognitive and psychometric assessments, we’re building the evidence needed to strengthen force health protection,” said army neurologist Lieutenant Colonel Antony Sutherland, a member of the study team. The royal commission, released in 2024, found that traumatic brain injuries are associated with a heightened risk of death by suicide in veteran and civilian populations. “Traumatic brain injury from blast exposure is common in active-duty military personnel,” the final report found. “Many researchers believe that the pressure wave passing through the brain significantly disrupts brain function, causing damage.”



The royal commission found current and ex-service members “reported receiving insufficient support from the ADF for brain injury and having difficulty obtaining compensation”. If you are a current or former ADF member or a relative and need counselling or support, contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046.
